utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Tuesday, June 17th, 2008, and I greet the representatives of the OTP, Mr. Seselj, as well as everyone helping us. We are here to continue the hearing of our witness. It's the cross-examination now. Mr. Seselj sent us a number of documents which he intends to use during this cross-examination, and the OTP also has the documents or can have the documents. We will now bring the witness into the courtroom. Could the usher please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me? Very well. The cross-examination will now start, and I will give the floor to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, we're going to begin with the events in the village of Svrake. You lived in that village when the conflict broke out between the Serbian and Muslim armies, and the conflict lasted two days; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the Muslims, although they were perhaps less well armed than the Serbs and the JNA, did not wish to surrender right up until the JNA Air Force appeared looming above the village; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't say that during your examination-in-chief, but I learned that four bombs were dropped on the village from the plane.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nobody was killed by those bombs, but they did frighten the Muslim soldiers, and after that they decided to surrender; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: During the fighting in the village of Svrake, just one Muslim soldier was killed; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I have some information that tells me that one soldier was killed. But, anyway, you lived in the village of Svrake with your family, and when the conflict broke out, you asked a neighbour of yours, who was a Muslim, to put your wife and small child up in his cellar, which served as a shelter; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he refused; he said there wasn't any room; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what do you think, did he refuse you just because there was actually no room or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there was no room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how many people were in that cellar?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go in to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you don't know how many people were in his cellar?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Wasn't it logical, if you asked for your wife and small child, for him to say, "Well, let them come into the cellar and I'll stay outside"? Isn't that what any honourable man would have done?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What's your neighbour's name?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mizet Piknjac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mizet Piknjac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Sejdic, later on, you found -- happened to be in the Muslim village of Korita; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where you came by buses?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how many days did you stay in the village?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifteen to twenty days, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And why were only you returned to Semizovac and nobody else?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly why they sent me back. Probably because I was a Roma.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because you were a Roma, they had this antipathy towards your family and you. Usually, Bosnian Muslims call the Roma "Gurbeti"?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you hear that one of these people who told you you had to leave said, "All we need is Gurbetis over here"?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't hear that, okay. But you told the Serbs that when you arrived in Semizovac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not how I put it. That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So which Muslims in Korita told you that you had to go to Semizovac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't know the names of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, some people came and said, "You have to go to Semizovac," right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how was it, then?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said, "Anybody who wants to go to Semizovac and Sarajevo, there's a free place down there. You can pass through. Nobody will do anything to you." That's what we heard. And then my father decided that we should start off towards Sarajevo because we have some family there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your father went to Sarajevo, but you went to Semizovac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My family and my father and all of us went towards Semizovac, and if we wanted to go to Sarajevo, we had to go to Semizovac. And there were paramilitary units there, Serbs, Serb paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And in Semizovac, you joined a work unit and then a combat unit of the Serb Army, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not straight away. I didn't join straight away, but when we arrived in Semizovac, Nebojsa Spiric took us into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where did he take you into custody?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he took us to our houses, kept us in detention there, interrogated us, and took my brother away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your brother was in the Muslim units; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they knew about that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He took part in the fighting for Svrake?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they incarcerated him and then set him free a few days later?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't set him free. They allowed him to report to us at home, to tell us, and then put us in prison in Planina Kuce.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's look at this. He was free for two days, and then he left, and nobody ever learned where he went; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When he came to our house to tell us, he tried to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, is there any logic in them releasing him to go home for two days and then to have him back in prison? There's no logic there.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they did, they released them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They let him go home, and then he went somewhere after that, and you don't know where either; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He came to see us, and then later on he was supposed to report to the prison in Planina Kuce. A soldier came to fetch him. However, he tried to escape, and they captured him somewhere up there when they brought him to prison. They took him to Planina Kuce, and we never heard of him later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As a member of the Work Platoon, you had a salary, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, some little salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You had a salary?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't take any salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What did you live on?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we received some humanitarian aid from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the Red Cross or whatever. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You received financial assistance from the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were given a certain sum of money, which wasn't a large sum of money, by way of a salary, and every month you would get food issued to you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And your family lived on that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Life was difficult, but it was difficult for everyone else, too; they all lived the same way, right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And your wife, for that first year while you were doing your work assignment, became pregnant and gave birth, thank goodness, to a healthy child, alive and well?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, where did your wife give birth?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was she given all the medical assistance she needed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way, I wouldn't say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did she ask for any assistance and the Serb authorities withhold it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She didn't ask for assistance, nor did the Serb authorities come to our door.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You had the right to health insurance throughout the time that you were undergoing your work assignment?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you had that right; you had the right to health insurance, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have that right. If I did have that right, then the whole time I wouldn't have suffered. I would have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we haven't come to that suffering part, whether you suffered or not, yet. What I'm saying is of your own free will, you joined the Serb authorities, and then of your own free will, you became a member of a combat unit. Now, may we have on our screens document 0220-4652 on e-court, please. I assume e-court is working and the document can be put on e-court. The Prosecution provided me with it. If you don't have the document, then I'll give you my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one point for clarification. Mr. Seselj says that the witness voluntarily accepted to go with the Serb authorities, but during the examination-in-chief, he said that he was forced to go and this was against his will. Could Mr. Seselj please quote the source that he's using to say so, unless it's the document he's showing now or he will show?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj. It seems that there is a slight problem on the labour done in this unit. Was he forced to do it or did he do it of his own will, freely? You seem to say that he had a salary, but he says that he didn't want the salary. But all elements seem to show that he was free to go. Maybe the document will shed light on this and go in favour of what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to provide an explanation, but I hope that won't be deducted from my valuable time. A work obligation or assignment was prescribed by law in Serbia and Republika Srpska, and the Muslim Croatian Federation took over that law and the regulation. All citizens that weren't incorporated into their military training assignment were in the work assignment which is parallel to the military assignments, so if you weren't fit for a military assignment, you would have a work assignment, and it has the right to a salary, health insurance and so on. Certain rights are incurred on the basis of that status.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So on the basis of that work of yours in the work unit, you received a salary, you were supplied with food, and you had health insurance. Have you seen the document? This was issued by the Command of Military Post 749/12 to which you belonged; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So this is a certificate confirming that you were a member of the Army of Republika Srpska as of the 4th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what it says on the certificate. The OTP provided me with that. Whether that's correct, I'm not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it can say there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was deployed in the Semizovac Battalion, where he still is located, and this certificate is issued for the realisation of the rights to health and social insurance of family members. Wife, Kadira, born on such-and-such a date, and son, Edim, and daughter, Eldina. So on the basis of your work assignment, as members of your immediate family, your dependents had the right to social and health insurance, and this is proof -- the certificate was issued in 1994, when you needed it for some purpose?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not issued that certificate and this is the first time that I see that certificate. Now, what you're saying, that I had the right to all these entitlements, I didn't have that right straight away. This was towards the end of the war, and the fact that they gave us humanitarian assistance, they gave us that to help us survive because there was nobody else to work. We had to be alive in order to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now turn to page 2 of that document to see what it says there. So here we have a document from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia, Department Vogosca, with all the dates and numbers. The date is 1994, which also confirms that you, Mr. Sejdic, were a member of the Army of Republika Srpska from the 4th of April, 1992, and that this certificate is issued for you to realise your rights from the social and health insurance regulations, and members of your family, your wife, Kadira, your son, Edim, your daughter, Eldina, and this certificate cannot be used for other purposes. This was issued by the head of the department of Vogosca, the Ministry of Defence, Jovo Peranovic, and here we have your signature. You received that because that's your signature there confirming it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true, sir, that that is the date. I don't agree with this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my signature, yes, but what is typed up above is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. If the typing's not correct, then it was the wrong typewriter that was used, but I'm interested to know that that is your signature.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be anybody's.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1994, you yourself asked to become a member of a combat unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have a document here. It's not translated, but I think we can understand what this document is all about. It's a military document. On the left, there are references, numbers. There's a date, 11th of May, 1994. Then we also see your name. It says that since April 4th, 1992, you belonged to the VRS. And there's also mention of your relatives. And on the bottom left, this document seems to bear your own signature. Mr. Seselj has asked you whether this was your signature. You said, "Yes, it is," after which you said something else. So I'll ask the question myself. Does this document bear your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my signature, but it's not the date, and not all this is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you sign this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was signed in 1994, going on 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It seemed that it was signed on May 11, 1994. At least that's the date that seems to be written next to your signature. If the document was signed in 1994 by you, it has to do with something that happened before 1994. And by signing this document, you authenticated what was written above. So there are two possibilities. Either what we have here is a forged document or what you signed here does not correspond to what is written.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text here -- well, the dates don't correspond to the text, and what's typed out here, as far as I can see, not everything is correct, because what they're saying here is that from 1992 until 1995, when I agreed to be their soldier. I never agreed to be their soldier, nor was I their soldier, from 1992, but that was from 1994 and the end of 1995, when they forced me to become one of their soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... I didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution has the document in English, and it's up to them to show you the original, because I was disclosed the document by the OTP and I see the -- you can see the ERN number, which means that it should be on e-court. Now, why it's not on e-court, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Anyway, Mr. Sejdic, do you know who Meho Osmanovic is?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know who Meho Osmanovic is. He's my neighbour who was in the work platoon with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And this man, Meho Osmanovic, was considered to be a decent, honest man; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Meho Osmanovic, in 1995, gave a statement to the sector of the state security, the Ministry of the Interior for the Muslim part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so may we have 03487511 document, please, up on our screens? It's the ERN number, you haven't got it? What is the Prosecution doing, I have to do their work for them. Now, you're going to show page 1 of the document for us to see the date, and then page 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. This document comes from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we reviewed the documents in order to find exculpatory documents, we disclosed these documents to Mr. Seselj, and then it's up to Mr. Seselj to upload them into e-court, if he wishes to. This is not up to the OTP to do this. The OTP just has to disclose them under Rule 66(B) or 68 and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This means that this document was not up-loaded into e-court by the OTP. We have it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I received this document from the OTP a week ago, a week ago, and that is when they were supposed to upload it into the e-court system. How could I do that? I know how to drive a nail into a wall, but to drive this into a computer, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and to Dr. Seselj. This issue has come up several times and we want to make it very clear that it's not our job to upload documents into e-court for Mr. Seselj. If he wants documents uploaded into e-court, then he needs to take whatever steps or arrangements have been made with the Registry in order to do that. The fact that we disclose material does not mean that we upload it into e-court for his use. It's up to the parties to make sure that material is uploaded into e-court, and if Dr. Seselj needs some training on that, then we can certainly arrange for that to be done, but it's not our job to upload Defence documents into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But independently of this, at the OTP do you have the English translation of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which document are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you out of the blue. When we see some documents, some are in B/C/S without translation, and we have a language assistant that could help us and can make a side translation of it, and then we can decide whether it is exculpatory or not. So a document disclosed to Mr. Seselj in B/C/S will not necessarily have an English translation. I can check this, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another mystery. This document that's of May 18, 1995, and I think I understood that Mr. Seselj just got it a few days ago. Why is it that such an old document was only disclosed to Mr. Seselj a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This person making the statement is not on our witness list. When searches are made to try and find exculpatory material using the names of future witnesses, then sometimes documents crop up, and this is when we review them and disclose them in due time. Mr. Seselj obtained this document in due time and can use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I always have the most time at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sejdic, let us look at the cover page of this document. We see the number, the date. We see that it's marked "Official Secret, Strictly Confidential." Can we have a look at page 17 now? I think it's 17. Let us see what this man says, for whom we stated that he was an honest man in your community: "I claim that --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: " ... he took part in the Chetnik formations from the Intervention Platoon of the Semizovac Battalion. He took part in fighting at Mount Zuc and in some fighting at the localities during the course of 1993 and 1994. I personally saw him carrying the PM-84." That is that sower of death, right, that machine-gun, PM-84? "And I heard that Vaske Vidovic, because of his good actions in the Chetnik units, called him to join him, that is to say, to join the formation that he commanded." Is this man stating the truth, Mr. Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this is not correct. And what Mr. Meho is saying is what you brought up here in writing with your own notes. That is your procedure and that is how you always defend yourself, with such procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you think I wrote this document?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who wrote this document, but this was never true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Is this your suspicion, that Meho, whatever his last name is --

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: -- that he made this kind of statement?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meho Osmanovic was with me in the work platoon. I know that. As for such statements made by him, that he claimed that this was true, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please let us look at the signature. Meho Osmanovic, he signed every page. Is this his signature?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't go to school with Meho, so it's not that I knew what his signature was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I think that you can give that kind of answer, I respect that answer of yours, but do you think that I fabricated this document in order to expose you to some embarrassment?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we are not here on account of Meho Osmanovic but on account of you and all the members of your groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We're here because of you, Mr. Sejdic, as well.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All of what you say are lies.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of what you're saying are lies. If you say that I carried a death sower --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, let's not have a debate here with the accused. Please do not debate with the accused, basically. You have the first page of the document. Please, can we see the first page? Very well. Witness, please look at this document attentively. This document was made on the 18th of May, 1995, apparently; in other words, right after the conflict. It's a statement that was taken on that date, and this person, who is your neighbour, he states some facts. Why would you say that in 1995, he says this about you, because in fact Mr. Seselj has nothing to do with this whole story on the 18th of May, 1995? So an investigation was carried out by the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Sarajevo sector, and this is what we can see on top. So, in other words, nothing in favour of Mr. Seselj. And this Meho Osmanovic states these facts. Why would he say that? This is what we're trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for this document, I am aware of this Meho Osmanovic, but I don't know who he gave the statement to. As for Meho Osmanovic, he was on the work platoon, and afterwards, in 1995, he did see me with Rajko Jankovic and his unit, as I have already pointed out. I had to do what Rajko told me to do. I did not kill people, I did not slit people's throats, but I did carry a weapon and I did follow him. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So you do admit that you bore weapons. That's new. That's a new fact, isn't it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you bore weapons that you had on you. Did you carry the PM-84, the death device or the death sower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was a PM of Mr. Rajko Jankovic. I carried his weapon and walked behind him. When he went into action, he used the weapon to shoot, not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this is what you told us in chief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I pointed that out. When I was a member of that unit of theirs, that I walked behind Rajko Jankovic and I carried his weapon; and not only his weapon but the weapons belonging to all the others. Whoever found anything heavy, they'd give it to me to carry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry to intervene, but very briefly. Line 12, once again page 16, line 12, there were some inappropriate statements regarding lies. This was already discussed earlier. I will not go into why this is inappropriate, but this should stop and Mr. Seselj should stop mentioning lies. This is causing pressure for the witness that is here and also for the future witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Chamber told you, Mr. Seselj, not to mention lies, not to accuse the witnesses of lying. The Chamber is working on a decision, and from now on the Trial Chamber will redact every time you mention such words. So once again, you are notified. We are asking you to avoid using those words. You have a document. You can put questions to the witness, and if you want to state the witness is not saying the same thing as the document, you can mention it, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to know the following: Do you know, when this statement was given, in what conditions was it given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, but I would like to know if you knew that an investigation was carried out as to the people who took part voluntarily or not in the war, who were Muslim and who may have participated within Serb forces. I would like to know if this statement may have been taken in that context or in those conditions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly whether this statement was taken in that way, because I don't know about Meho and the others who were on the work platoon with me, when they were examined and when they made statements. I haven't seen that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you knew that investigation was carried out in 1995, investigation carried out by the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When the war ended, the CSB, that's what it was called in Sarajevo, they would bring in people -- I mean their services that worked worked on the basis of these statements, and they brought in myself and other people who had been prisoners to make statements as to what happened when the village of Svrake was attacked and the other villages from 1992 up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this is not after the war. The date here is the 18th of May, 1995. Are you aware if an investigation was carried out on or about that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly. I really could not say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am so astonished by what you said a few moments ago that I can hardly recover. I did not tell the witness that he was lying. It's the witness who said that I was lying. And now you are attacking me on account of that. A few times, you told me that I'm not supposed to say that a witness is lying, although the basic proposition of my Defence case is that the Prosecution appears here with false witnesses and false propositions. I understood your threat. I'm always going to say in this courtroom that the Judges are very honourable people, the Prosecutors are even more honourable, and the witnesses are the most honourable of all, and I am the only one who lies in this courtroom. And I'm going to keep pointing that out all the time, so I'm going to do that all the time. There's no need for you to caution me about that anymore. But this is really astonishing. I never said to this witness that he is lying. He said that I was resorting to lies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, the speaker is speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, maybe there was an interpretation error. The Prosecutor may have understood or misunderstood that you were accusing him of lying. You may be right in what you've stated, but I was not only thinking about this particular case or instance. The Chamber does not want you to mention all the time that the witness is a false witness. We will see that in due time when we assess the statements and when we have to evaluate the probative value, but for now we don't know. We have a witness who is here, who is giving us a certain version of facts, and then we have another witness, giving us another version of facts, the only difference being that the witness before us is under oath. The other witness is not under oath, and that's a difference, but there's a contradiction. This witness tells us that he bore arms, whereas the other witness states that he was shooting with the unit, so that's the basic difference. Maybe he is telling the truth, maybe he is lying. I don't know. But it's after evaluating all the elements that we have that we will be able to establish the facts, and at this point in time it is premature to say that this witness is a false witness or not. We don't know at this point in time who is the false witness and who is not, and it is through cross-examination that you will be able to assess the credibility of the witness and that you will be able to put questions as to the substance of the case. This cross-examination started, it is not over yet, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is an inappropriate way of interrupting my cross-examination. From this moment onwards, I've already told you, for me all the witnesses here are truth-loving people. Everybody's telling the truth except for me; I'm a liar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, I, as a liar, ask Mr. Sejdic whether that means that he never had a weapon issued to him, this M-84, the machine-gun that is called the death sower? You were never issued with this weapon as your own?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never issued with this weapon as my own, unless I carried Rajko's weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you never had one issued to you in your own name?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have another statement here of a very honourable and honest man. Could you show this to the witness? I'm sure they don't have this in e-court, ER025349. I find this number to be strange, so we're just going to quote a small paragraph from that statement. This is a statement made by an honourable man whose name is Kasim Sejdic. That is your father; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please, the part that I marked, this is what -- oh, just take it back. Let us see the date of this statement. This is a statement made by your father on the 14th of March, 1996, to the Centre of the Security Services in Sarajevo. That is when the Muslim Army had already taken Ilijas, Vogosca and Ilidza. Now, scroll back down, and I'm now going to quote this paragraph. This is what your father says: "My son, Safet Sejdic, born in 1969, was mobilised by the Chetniks in the Army of Republika Srpska in 1994, and they issued to him a machine-gun, M-84 (death sower), and he went to the frontlines at the hill of Zuc, towards Visnjica and elsewhere. During 1995, he held the lines at Lipa, facing Srednje. He was in the Serb Army until February 1996. He received cigarettes and a salary from time to time." This is what your father stated. Could you scroll down so that we see the signature? Is this your father's signature?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father would never say something like this. These are lies. You will never prove to me that my father said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Am I the one who's lying here? Feel free to say so.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. My father didn't do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since I'm the only liar in this courtroom, then I am the one who lied about this, who typed this up falsely and falsified your father's signature?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this document bears the signature of your father. Your father seems to confirm what we have seen up until now, that is, that you were on the frontlines and that you had the M-84 weapon. Maybe the person who drafted this drafted this the way it is drafted, but when we read this, coming from your father, we are under the impression that your father says that you were a member of the VRS. He didn't say that you were forced to be a member. Didn't your father ever tell you that he was heard as part of an investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My father never -- my father never said this to me, and I don't know of my father mentioning this, my father saying that I was a member of all of this, that I carried weapons, whatever. He knows full well that my father was with me, and my father knows all the suffering that I went through and all the suffering that he went through; that is to say, whenever I went to the frontline following Mr. Rajko Jankovic and the rest from his Intervention Platoon, he also carried shells, ammunitions, just like I did, so I carried Rajko's weapons. So perhaps when he saw this and when they questioned him, maybe he said that, that I carried this weapon. But all of this, I don't know, really. I really find all of this to be something that I don't know, all these writings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, according to me, the only thing that should be clarified is whether you were mobilised or not. That's what I heard in the translation or interpretation. The fact that you worked with the Serb forces on the frontline, which is what you told us during the examination-in-chief, you told us that you bore weapons for a person for whom you worked, you accompanied that person to the frontline, you carried his weapon, so that's nothing new. It's not in contradiction with what you said previously. Now, if you were mobilised because you wanted to go and fight on that side, that's the question, or if there was a forced mobilisation. This is what we should clarify. Maybe it's impossible to clarify that point while reading this statement. I don't know, because I don't speak B/C/S, but would you please try to tell us exactly and precisely what is written on that first line on the document after your date of birth? We can read here "Cetnici su mobilizovali." Is this what we can read here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what is written there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could you please tell us what this means in your daily language, in the language that you understand on a daily basis? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here, allegedly, that I was issued this M-84.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The word "zaduzili," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Issued, "zaduzili," to take weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, when an army mobilises someone, does that mean that this army is mobilising only those who are already recruited or not? In other words, I would like to know if, by reading this, we can understand that you were mobilised on a voluntary basis or were you forced to join in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was forced to join that army. This was in 1995, the end of 1995, when they gave me that weapon, and I stated that. In my statement, I said I was a member of their unit, the Intervention Platoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So from this statement, we cannot clearly understand if this was a forced mobilisation or a volunteer mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The mobilisation was forced mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this is not what we have here on the document; right? It's not written. There's the benefit of the doubt. We don't know; right? But from reading this document, we cannot infer that you were mobilised as a volunteer, on a voluntary basis of your own free will, and that you were not forced to join the forces. We don't know; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, I said it correctly, when I was mobilised and when they gave me a weapon. I did not accept it of my own free will. They forced me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, when it says that you were issued the machine-gun known as "death sower," the M-48 [as interpreted], that means that you sign a receipt with your name, and that's what every soldier does when he's issued a weapon?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Jankovic gave it to me, and I said that at the beginning, when I was a member and when they gave it to me, and I had to because they threatened me. He personally said all sorts of things to me. I know that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At one point, with this machine-gun, you could have killed his whole unit?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you think he put a whole round of bullets in my -- a whole clip in my machine-gun. He just gave me a few bullets, and he kept asking me where the Muslims are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, I use the second-person plural, which is the proper way to address somebody. You have used the second-person singular, you have used the "tu" instead of the "vous" in addressing me, so I'm asking you to address me in the proper way, please. Now, tell me, Mr. Sejdic, why would your father tell the Muslim authorities that you had been issued this machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my father stated this and gave this statement, then he had to say -- well, he had -- they had the statements, he had to say it that way, which means my father did not lie. He gave the statement because he knew that I carried Jankovic's machine-gun, that I escorted him, followed him, and that I carried the gun for him. He knows that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, you know in this last paragraph of that statement, your father says that: "My words are included in the statement, and I recognise it as being my own, and I sign it with my own hand." Is that your father's signature there at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you see that Nedim Curevac, an employee of the city, took this statement, the clerk, and the recorder was Jasna Pasovic? Very well, Mr. Sejdic. Now, we've finished with the document. You can take it away. But is it true that the Muslim authorities arrested you at the beginning of March 1996, after taking over control of that part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arrested me, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that the Muslims arrested me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they take you into detention and took you to the State Security Station?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was when the blue route was open, the convoy known as the blue convoy, when the Muslims were going back to Semizovac and Vogosca. That's when I was taken to the CSB, as it was called, the Centre of Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did they find on you an ID -- a military booklet of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I handed over my military booklet and told them the whole truth, how it happened and what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who did you hand your military booklet over to?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Of the Muslim Croatian Federation?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the next document be put on the overhead projector, 00397418. I assume that you don't have this on e-court, either, so we're going to look at page 1 and what it says at the top. 00397418 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is your statement which you gave on the 14th of March, 19 -- or, rather, the 16th of March, 1996, to the Centre of Security Services, the CSB, and you can see here that it says this: " ... is in possession of a military booklet issued by the military post 7033/15 Vogosca by the Army of the so-called Republika Srpska." And then it goes on to say that your personal ID number was recorded there and so on, and what it is. So that's the military post that you denied. Were you a member of that military post?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. I have absolutely no idea about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have no idea; right. Now, do you know who Dragan Gavric is?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know who Dragan Gavric is?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's very strange, because he knows you. So let's have document number 7. I sent it in to you this morning. Dragan Gavric, nicknamed Kele. Did you know somebody who was nicknamed Kele?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. If you don't know, let's see, because he knows you well. This is a statement that arrived a moment ago, given by this Dragan Gavric, aka Kele, who listened to your testimony on Thursday. I don't know him, but he contacted my expert team and gave this statement that was authenticated in the administrative service of Bijeljina municipality on the 13th of June. That's where he went to certify it, and I was faxed this this morning. Here's what it says, what Dragan Gavric, also known as Kele, says: "I know Safet Sejdic very well because we slept in next-door beds in the dormitory of the Intervention Platoon of the Semizovac Battalion in Svrake village which was always on the alert in order to respond to the BH Army attacks." Do you remember that man now, this man Dragan Gavric?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, and these documents that you're being sent, I don't know how you come by them, how you're being sent them. Anyone can be sent documents like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, everything that we've looked at so far are documents provided to me by the OTP, including your father's statement.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This document is not correct. I don't know about any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you a sportsman, yourself?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't a sportsman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You weren't a sportsman; right? Anyway, Dragan Gavric says that you were a good fighter, and here it says in paragraph 4: "I know exactly that in those battles, he killed a total of ten enemy Muslim soldiers."

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then he goes on to comment on your testimony in The Hague. We're not interested in that, so we'll skip that over. And then he goes on to say -- Dragan Gavric goes on to say: "I can testify that on the 23rd of February, 1996," and he's talking about you now -- "he was facing a great dilemma, whether to withdraw with the Serbian population, but he stayed on nonetheless, and this resulted in terrible torture and beating by his Muslim neighbours after they had taken control of Semizovac." Now, is that true? Were you beaten by the Muslim authorities when they captured you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, gentlemen, Judges, none of it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean it's not true that they beat you when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're putting to me now in all those questions, and putting to me something about some Dragan and what he said, I have no idea who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, he gives us his particulars. He lives in Djureva Jaksic [phoen] Street, Bijeljina, he certified the statement. Now, I've never met him, I've never seen him, but you say you don't know him. Very well.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm astonished how you managed to come by this document, because it seems that everybody gets these documents and sends them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you don't imagine that I'm going to explain how I get my documents. I get them from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how you -- can you ask me these questions, do I know this and do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know Mujo Djafic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know Faruk Djafic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now you don't wish to know anyone, I see, as of now on. All right. Do you know who Miroslav Spiric is?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Spiric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean Nebojsa Spiric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, this is Miroslav Spiric.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Miroslav Spiric. Perhaps that's his father, Nebojsa's father.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He says that he's a neighbour of yours and that your house is just a hundred metres away from his own and that he's known you from birth. May we have statement number 8 placed on our screens, please. This is what Miroslav Spiric says, and he now lives in Zvornik. This is what he says, here we are: "I can state that Mr. Safet Sejdic was not forcibly mobilised, nor was anybody from Semizovac or after Svrake being handed over. Everybody could go where they wanted, and Svrake --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe there's a problem here regarding this -- but as of document 8-1, I have no certification on the page. Maybe I'm missing a page, maybe there should be a second page with a certification page that I don't have, unless -- I apologise. There is a second page, but the certification is not on the document itself, and because of this I didn't make the connection. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The certification is on the back of the document, and when I am faxed this, then it has to be on two pieces of paper, not on one. Anyway, you say you don't know him, whereas he seems to know you very well.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement, the statement that he says he -- in which he says he knows me, well, we weren't voluntarily -- or, rather, that means we voluntarily applied to be members of your army. If we were free, we wouldn't be with you; we would be on the Muslim side with the Muslims, had we been free.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you already left with the Muslims. You were in Korita, Mr. Sejdic, and then the Muslims didn't want to take you in. They sent you away. They said denigrating things to you and called you "Gurbetis," that's another phrase for the Roma, but that's what the Muslims in Bosnia call you, the "Gurbeti."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're speaking way too fast and we're losing track of what you're saying, so please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were already with the Muslims in Korita and the Muslims sent you away, they didn't want to have you amongst them, and they called you all sorts of derogatory names, they called you a "Gurbeti" and referred to you as "Gurbeti" and said they didn't want any "Gurbetis" there, and then you went to the Serb side and everybody says you were a brave fighter?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I was brave when you wanted me to bring in your dead and to follow Jankovic, to carry his weapons. So I suffered a great deal from you, so don't keep talking to me about things like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You came here to testify of your own free will, and you're going to have to take this to the end even if you find it unpleasant.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will take it all, because I'm right. Now, what you're saying, I'm not going to say what you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your neighbour, Miroslav Spiric, in paragraph 4, let's zoom down that page a little, says that: "Safet Sejdic, throughout the war, was voluntarily on the same side, and in 1994, he left to join the Intervention Platoon at his personal request, where he took part in the most complicated actions and operations. Throughout this time from 1992, he was on the payroll of the Army of Republika Srpska. And I can confirm that because I was the main administrative person in the battalion. And also, Safet Sejdic, throughout the time, took his meals in Kulin Dvor Cafe and was given his regular amount of cigarettes. The Kulin Dvor Cafe was where the Command was, and the restaurant was on the ground floor, where food was issued on a regular basis." Is what Miroslav Spiric says here true?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and as far as I understand what you're talking about, about the food and the cigarettes, when we went to work they would give us a packet of cigarettes, when we deserved it, that is. And I think that I say that in one of my statements, that I say that when we went to the frontline and when we did something well, they would give us food and let us go and visit our wives and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, this man, Miroslav Spiric, also tried to stay in Vogosca when the Serbs withdrew. Although he's a Serb, he wanted to stay in his own house. However, this is what happened to him, and he says that in the next paragraph. He says: "I am one of the unfortunates who believed that peace had been signed and that the situation would return to normal. However, on the 13th of May, 1996, members of the BH Army, under the leadership of Nail Gajovic, beat me black and blue, me and my wife. They even broke my left leg and two of my ribs, and there are documents to prove it, recording it. And I also have to state that after they entered it, after Dayton, the soldiers of the BH Army completed devastated the Serb cemetery. And as far as my son is concerned, whom Safet Sejdic mentioned, they destroyed the monument to him. Safet Sejdic might have fared even worse than me, because they also mistreated him badly and beat him up a lot, these same men, and Sejdic's mother, Razija, told me about that. So Sejdic, because of the beatings, had to spend a couple of months in hospital and barely survived. After such bad beatings which Sejdic survived, I'm not surprised at the way he's testifying." So there you have it. Miroslav Spiric claims that you were brutally beaten and mistreated and that your mother, Razija, told him about that, herself. Is that true and correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you trying to congratulate me, to calm me down in this way, reading this out?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why should I try to calm you down? I'm not a psychiatrist. I'm here to cross-examine you.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, but why would Spiric stay on in Semizovac if he was in the Serb Army and if he was one of the main people there? Why would he stay on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because the peace agreement was signed and he expected the situation to return to normal. He did not commit any crime or anything else, so why would he be afraid?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if he knew that his son had committed that act, how could he stay on there, just like I could not remain there had I done whatever on the Muslim side? Nobody would want to take me in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: His son was killed in the war. You mentioned his son, and he was killed during the war.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Nebojsa Spiric was killed and that he was quite aggressive, both before the war and during the war. For his father to be able to stay on there after that, I don't know how that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why wouldn't his father be able to stay on there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody knows why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was a criminal before the war and he was a criminal during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean his father?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why does Miroslav Spiric, his father -- well, everything you're saying about his son is not true, but that's not important now. Now, what would the reason be for Miroslav Spiric not to be able to stay in Vogosca, where his son's grave is located and where his house is located? Why wouldn't he stay in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a Serb would always defend a Serb and go with a Serb. A Serb wouldn't stay on with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He wanted to stay, but they beat him up?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that I wanted to stay with the Muslims, but I didn't, which means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness explained several times why Mr. Spiric's father could not stay. The question is being put to him repetitively, and I raise an objection here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, I was listening to you, and a small detail seems to crop up in this statement made by your neighbour, Miroslav Spiric. He states that he was beaten by the Muslim Army, he was beaten as well as his wife, and he is saying this, and he doesn't seem to be the only one. Seemingly, his wife also says so. But he adds a small detail which may have escaped most of you, but I noted it down. He says that you were also beaten and you had to spend some months in hospital after that. So is it true that you did spend months in hospital or is he lying, is it false?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, well, this statement -- I mean, I know his father, but what he's saying here, that I was in the hospital, that I was not in hospital, I was at home, when I was beaten up, when the lines fell and whatever, and what they are saying about him and his wife, that he was beaten so badly, I don't know. I wasn't there, so I cannot know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that you were not beaten by the Muslim forces. Very well, but my question is the following: Did you go to the hospital, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed, please, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where were you in May 1996?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May 1996? I don't know what kind of a question this is, where I was in May 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The question is a very nice one. I'll have to repeat it. Where were you in May 1996?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does this question mean, who, what, why?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where were you in May 1996?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in May 1996, it's true that if I was asked the same question, I would not know where I was, I would be unable to answer, but you might have a better memory than I do. So answer the question, please. He is asking you where you were in May 1996. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall the exact date. Where was I in May 1996? I guess it was the end of the war, and I was on the Muslim side in Semizovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In May 1996, you were in hospital; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, some hospital.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You weren't?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please be so kind as to take this photograph that accompanies this document. Perhaps this one is better than the other one. I expect my associates to send the original colour photograph by e-mail and that Mr. Doraiswamy is going to get this. I hope that my associates are following this and that they will send it during the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could have the colour copy later on, maybe we could wait for it, because it would be more legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what colour would add to this. We have a group of people here with weapons, a group of men with weapons. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sejdic said that he remembered this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you recognise yourself in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recognise myself in this photograph. I'm the first one here in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The first one on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're holding an automatic rifle in your hand; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They gave it to me so that they could take a picture of me. If that were to mean that it was the end of the war, if they didn't have time to kill me, then they would have the Muslims kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they took that kind of picture of you on purpose in order to stigmatize you before the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they expect the Serbian forces to leave Ilijas, Vogosca and Ilidza, and did they expect the entire population to leave, and did they expect the Muslim Army to come there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they expected that, that means that if they left documents and pictures of this kind, they wanted to leave all sorts of things against me because I knew a lot about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why would they lie anything about you when you were a hero in the Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I was just a hero if I carried your stuff. That's why they called me "Hero."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were a type of hero of socialist labour; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what that means, "socialist." What does "socialist" mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Socialist labour, volunteer work for the community without remuneration.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it wasn't voluntary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why did you need an automatic rifle, then, for this work? Were you cleaning the dust with this rifle or what?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Take a careful look at this rifle, whether it's been given to me loaded or not. Can you see a clip?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You can see a clip here.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see better, then. Are there bullets in that rifle? Did they give that kind of rifle to me? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we saw from your father's statement that later on you were even given an M-84, issued with one.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I pointed out in my own statements, I carried Jankovic's weapon, not my own. It wasn't my own. This is who was carrying an M-84, Jovan Colakovic, he's right next to me, and he told me a thousand times, and he hit me and he shouted at me, saying what I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He hit you, and you stand next to him to have your picture taken?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to stand next to my mother and father and have my picture taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why would you stand next to the man who hit you? No one ever laid a finger on you. What about karate, martial arts? Aren't you well versed in that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a lie too. You're lying again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I'm lying. I'm the only one here who is lying. At least that is something here we all concur on, the Trial Chamber, the OTP and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, no, there is no consensus, and I will state it over and over again. Witness, you are telling us that you're in civilian clothes and bearing a weapon. This Jankovic, is it the person on your right, if I'm not mistaken? I believe so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is Colakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where is this Jankovic person on the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Jankovic is not here. These are his soldiers who had their picture taken in front of the Command. This is the platoon, his platoon and -- well, where the trucks were, the trucks. It was something like the rolling stock or whatever it was called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Jankovic is not on the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jankovic is not in the photograph. I think he was at the Command then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this photograph, I see that you are dressed in plain clothes, but I also note, as far as the others are concerned, some are in camouflage dress, others in less obvious clothes. None have any headgear, except for the very -- for one at the very back of the picture with a helmet. We note that all members of this group seem quite young. Most carry weapons, except for the first one, but we can't see very well. He doesn't seem to have any weapons, just a tripod for a machine-gun, but you can't see it. According to what you're saying, the weapon that you are bearing was not loaded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, Mr. Seselj. You have ten minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, there's something that might have escaped me. You might have already said this, but I would like to know whether -- where and when this photograph was taken, if you remember this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This photograph was taken in front of the Command in Semizovac, facing Kulin Dvor, where the rolling stock was. That is where the picture was taken, and that is when Jovan Colakovic, the man standing right next to me with this automatic rifle, 84 -- I mean the 84 one, that's what they call it. He has these bandoliers on and this rifle. He personally brought me there and put the rifle in my rifle so that that is how I would have my picture taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give us a date, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember exactly. I think it was towards the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This photograph was taken the spring of 1994; isn't that right, Mr. Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, as I've pointed out just now. Towards the end of the war, that's when it was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have military trousers on and boots?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These are rubber boots and old, dirty jeans, and a sort of T-shirt or shirt. It was dirty as well. You can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, why would this group of soldiers force you to have their picture taken with you; in order to embellish their picture or what?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they knew that I would come here or whatever, wherever some day. They wanted to prove the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since you were an ethnic Roma, the only one in that unit, were there any Croats in that unit?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember Ninoslav Kaurinovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kaurinovic was a Croat, but he was not there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ninoslav Kaurinovic is the person who kept this photograph, and he sent it to me. Now we are going to see what his statement says. Could we please have document number 6 now. He came to Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, are you going to ask for this photograph to be tendered?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Judge. You know that I'm not going to tender anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will consult my fellow Judges to see whether this photograph could be a Bench exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could we please have a number for this photograph as a Bench exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit number C2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we make sure that Mr. Seselj also gives us the colour photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if we have a colour copy, that would be even better. Proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No need, since the witness recognised the photograph, there's no need for me to provide a better one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please, this is very brief, and I hope we're going to deal with it by the time the break begins. Ninoslav Kaurinovic, son of Ante, a Croat, a Roman Catholic, and he came to Belgrade to make a statement on behalf of my Defence, because he wants the truth to be told. He made some comments with regard to some of the things you said during the examination-in-chief. He says for himself: "I was a member of the Army of Republika Srpska from the moment the Semizovac Battalion was established. I was a soldier of the 2nd Squad of the 2nd Platoon of the Semizovac Company or the 5th Semizovac Battalion." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the man who made this statement was not there all the time because he was crazy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was what?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was crazy. He was sort of not right in the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why was he not right in the head; because he was in the Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was that way before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you have proof of that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I have proof of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the basis of what do you assess that someone is crazy or not right in the head?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
