utterances.text: Because that's the way he always behaved, and I'm surprised that he is making a statement and saying that he knows everything. He was there like a crazy man, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, this is what Ninoslav Kaurinovic says: "I know that my neighbours, Semka Zukic and her daughter, were never brought into custody or detained, and that throughout the war they were in Semizovac. Semka worked as a waitress at the Social Centre of Semizovac." So she is challenging what you said: "I know for sure that the soldiers and officers from our unit were not in any way linked to the killing of civilians, which I confirm with full responsibility, and I know personally that Commander Rajko Jankovic, his deputy Nenad Kuzmanovic, and the security man, Rajko Rajic, protected them and took care of them. As an inhabitant of Semizovac and as a soldier, I know with certainty that Vaske Vidovic never entered any one of the buildings of the prison in Vogosca. I've lived in Semizovac since I was born, and I know that there were never any mosques in Semizovac and Kamenica. As for the fighting that took place at the Niksic Plateau that I participated in as well, I can only say that we participated just in the fighting around the village of Zubet. This happened at the beginning of November 1993 around Mitrovdan, and I remember that Srdjan Maunaga got killed and that Ranko Simic, Jovan Colakovic and Safet Sejdic were prominent in that battle." Is this true?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who destroyed the mosque in Semizovac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, half of them were destroyed by planes and the other half by Vaske.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You see that Ninoslav Kaurinovic says that in Semizovac, there were never any mosques?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, see for yourself whether there is a mosque there and whether there was ever a mosque there. You can check.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They say that there was never a mosque in Semizovac, and the Prosecutor can check that, since you are a Prosecution witness. They can check that out and they can give you information by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ninoslav Kaurinovic, had he written this, since he lived in Semizovac for so many years, he would have known that there is a mosque in Svrake and that there was always a mosque in Svrake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Svrake, yes, it is almost an exclusively Muslim village, but in Semizovac there was never a mosque, and that is what I claim too.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, Semizovac, Svrake, all of that was under Vogosca. Semizovac was just there across the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Semizovac and Svrake are two separate local communes in the municipality of Vogosca; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Separate local communes. In Svrake, there was a mosque; in Semizovac, there was never a mosque. And you said that an aeroplane destroyed the mosque in Semizovac and that it was polished off by Vaske Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Semizovac, well, I grew up there. As a child, I knew of Semizovac and Svrake. It's one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh, please, Mr. Sejdic. As for the village of Svrake, you praised it during the examination-in-chief. You even referred to it as a town. I even thought it was a metropolis. Didn't you say here that it was your native town, that you always considered it to be a town, that it looked like a town? It's in the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in the village of Svrake, but I did point out that I was born in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It doesn't matter where you were born. What is important is that in Semizovac there was never a mosque, and you claimed that there was a mosque and then that it was destroyed, first by an aeroplane and then finished off by Vaske Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Svrake and Semizovac is one and the same thing for me, and I don't know how to treat it in a different way. I don't know how to point this out. It was my own village. Semizovac, Svrake, Vogosca, that's where I lived, that's where I grew up, and I knew that there was a mosque in Svrake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I could say, for me, Addis Ababa and Kuala Lumpur are one in the same thing.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not a politician, like you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber did not go on the field. Normally, Trial Chambers go on the field, and we might go. But there's one point that you might shed light on immediately. Semizovac and Svrake, are these two villages that are side by side and that make up a single locality, or between -- is there any distance between Semizovac and Svrake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, that's another matter, that's a different question. From Semizovac to Svrake is just 100 metres or so. The village was called "Svrake," and the local commune of -- was Semizovac. It had its own local commune, and the village of Svrake had its own local commune. And the mosque was in Svrake village, so everybody was there in Semizovac from Semizovac, the Serb paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's take a break. It is 10.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break, could you instruct the Prosecutor to find, in these many statements by Safet Sejdic, there are five in all -- to locate in which of his statements Safet Sejdic talks about Ratko Mladic, Karadzic and me and our meeting on the eve of the attack on Niksic plateau and Crna Rijeka. As the witness during the examination-in-chief said that he stated that in all his statements, the Prosecutor didn't wish to remind him in which particular statement. Now, since I didn't find this in any of his statements, could you instruct the Prosecution to find that in those statements? And it can even be deducted from my time. I'm willing to have it deducted from my time, but I want them to find what statement that appears in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last week, just before the hearing ended, the witness told us that he had seen Mr. Seselj on this plateau with Karadzic and Mladic, but the accused told us that he did not see this in any statement. Was this said, in fact, or did you see this during the weekend?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to wonder why, and I insist on this, that it is not up to us to prepare Mr. Seselj's cross-examination, it's up to him. This is something that has to be very clear here. I, in fact, put the question as to when he had said this the first time, and the witness gave us an answer, and that was the end of that. And now it's up to Mr. Seselj to review all the documents and to see by himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 10.00, 10.15, actually. Mr. Seselj, you've used up 53 minutes so far, so unless I'm mistaken, you will have one hour and seven minutes left. Unless I am mistaken, that's what I say. And I will first ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom before we take a break, and the Trial Chamber will withdraw for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Very well. So the Trial Chamber will resume the hearing at 10.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please, let's have the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In the meantime, we were able to get the picture in colour, and we notice that the witness wore boots, a blue pair of trousers and a white shirt whereas most of the other people on the photo were wearing a camouflage uniform, with the exception of two people who wore a blue outfit. This is what this colour picture was able to show us. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would it be possible to replace the colour picture with the black-and-white picture? Maybe it's done automatically, or the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, very well. Mr. Registrar, could you please give us a number for the colour picture, C3.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number C3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Leave the photograph there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, do you know the names of all these soldiers on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I can't remember all of them just now. I know them all, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you point to Sladjan Okilj?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sladjan Okilj?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's Sladjan Okilj, is it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was killed; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So he died on the 24th of October, 1993; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the photograph was taken before his death; right? In the summer of 1993, in fact; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when he was killed, the actual moment, but this photograph was taken towards the end of the war, and I said "1994."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that this was towards the end of the war, and the war ended in 1995. Here we see Sladjan Okilj, he was alive and well, and was killed on the 24th of October, 1993. Therefore, this photograph must have been taken before the death of Sladjan Okilj. It was, in fact, taken in 1993 and not towards the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say towards the end of the war. I said "1994." I emphasise this. I didn't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, a moment ago you said the photograph was taken towards the end of the war and that they took the photograph and put you there to compromise you in the eyes of the Muslim authorities?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just as you, "tu," said a moment ago that I was wearing a uniform, and that's not what we see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please, I'm warning you once again to behave yourself and not address me with "tu," but "vous." And if the Trial Chamber doesn't want to tell you how to behave, then I have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I noticed that the interpreters were saying "tu" at some point, so I guess you spoke to Mr. Seselj by telling him "tu." So please tell him "vous," and that will avoid any further problems. But I also notice that the picture was not taken after the month of October 1993. It also seems almost certainly that this picture was taken during the summer, because you yourself are not wearing very warm clothes, so we can just imagine that this picture was taken from May to September, maybe even all the way through to October. Very well, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a minor point. If Mr. Seselj has a document testifying about the death of the person we are talking about, it would be perhaps better to shed some light on us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you told us that the soldier that we see here in the foreground in blue was killed on the 24th of October, 1993. You must base this on some facts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, didn't the witness confirm that? He said "October 1993." Then I reminded him and said, "The 24th of October," and he confirmed that it was the 24th of October, 1993. And now, instead of the Prosecution conducting an investigation, which it is duty-bound to do, it should have tested the credibility of all the witness statements beforehand. Now they're asking me to conduct an investigation. He was killed on the 24th of October, 1993. That is an indisputable fact. Anybody else claiming differently has to prove it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the photograph was taken before Okilj was killed, so it couldn't have been taken in 1996, just prior to the departure of the Serb Army from these territories. It couldn't have been taken in 1995, either, or in 1994, as you're trying to say now and correct yourself. The photograph must have been taken in 1993; right, Mr. Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, as far as this photograph is concerned, as far as I know, 1993, the end of 1993, going on to 1994, that's what I said in the first place. And, secondly, the photograph that you "tu" or, rather, you "vous" are saying about this man having been killed, I stressed a moment ago that he was killed then, but I don't remember, myself, what I had to eat when, let alone this photograph, because I didn't only have to think about a photograph at the time, I had to think about my life and the danger to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We see here that you still had a work assignment, work duty, not a military duty, but you had this photograph taken with the Semizovac Battalion, the elite battalion?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you said that I was a member of the army and that I took -- was taken with them, and there you have the evidence, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we've already established that I'm the biggest liar in this courtroom, and I couldn't see what I see now in the black-and-white photograph. But I have my associates, and they showed me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please don't say that. This is completely inappropriate. Witness, we see 20 people on this picture. Were there other people who were killed from this picture? If you know, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zvonko Maric was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were saying "this person." You have to show it to us with a stick, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. And another of them was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the pen, could you please put a cross above the person who was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks] [Interpretation] Do you want me to cross this out, the one I mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So three were killed, as far as you can remember. Can we have another number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The annotated photograph will be Exhibit number C4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What did you say these two soldiers' names were, the ones that were killed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one was called Zekic or something like that, Zeko or Zekic, and the other one was called --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said Zvonko Maric?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Zvonko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When were they killed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but after Okilj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So we're talking about 1993 now? You're not challenging that anymore now, are you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. We're not talking about a specific date. We're talking about the year. It was before October 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It could be 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how could it be 1994 if Sladjan Okilj was killed in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was killed before, before them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But he's on the photograph too. You don't assume that somebody brought in Dragan Okilj dead here to take a photograph of him in 1994, God forbid?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stress that he was killed afterwards, after the others. The question was whether any other people were killed after him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The question was: Is it -- is there no doubt that the photograph was taken in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the question was whether I knew anybody else who was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We've dealt with that. You recognised two other fighters who were killed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So is it indubitable that the photograph is 1993, was taken in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stressed this again, I said it a thousand times. I said the end of 1993, going on to 1994, and I can't remember everything exactly. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. But is it true and correct that this photograph, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, please. Mr. Seselj asked you, Witness, at one point if it is true that Okilj was killed in October of 1993. Unless the transcript is faulty, you've answered, "Yes." Now you say, "I don't know." I would like to know if you know, "yes" or "no," if that person was killed in the month of October 1993, because you did say, "Yes," at some point earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir, Witness, this question is for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said 1993, going on to 1994. I can't remember exactly, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I'm sorry, I didn't see that my colleague wanted to take the floor. I would like it to be clear on the audio, and we can verify this, when Mr. Seselj put the question to you as to whether it is true that he was killed in October of 1993, you said, "Yes," and then after that you said that you don't remember. But at one point in time earlier, you answered by saying, "Yes." So listen carefully to the questions that are put to you, because there are some discrepancies now and this has a certain bearing on the credibility. So please try to be more careful and be precise. Be careful when you listen to the questions and be precise when answering.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madame Judge, just a moment, please. A brief intervention. The first time I asked the witness when Sladjan Okilj was killed. The witness said in October 1993. Then I went on to ask him, "Was that on the 24th of October, 1993?" So October 1993 was a date first mentioned by the witness and then by me. So the witness answered correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, I think we can conclude that this photo was taken sometime before the 24th of October, and I'm not sure that we can get any further, but I have another question relating to the picture, because I see that the combatants here on this photo, they're all wearing a red band on their right shoulder. And my question is if you know what this red piece of ribbon or band signified. You can see on the picture that they all have, on their right shoulder, a piece of red ribbon. What is the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that. It was placed on the right shoulder when they were going to the Intervention Platoon, into an attack, that they could be distinguished by these bands or ribbons, and if anything happened during the night, that they could be recognised. They could recognise each other by these bands or ribbons and they would be able to recognise members of their unit which would have this mark.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, may I be of assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Sejdic, was the red ribbon only for this unit or were there other units carrying a similar ribbon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other units used this when they went into an attack, the same ribbons. They would have different ribbons, actually; sometimes yellow, sometimes blue, sometimes red. The colours would change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, unfortunately on this photograph we don't see if you, yourself, had this ribbon, because the weapon is hiding your right shoulder, so we can't see it. From memory, can you tell us if you as well wore the ribbon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not on that day. But when we went into an attack, then they would put this on my shoulder, please, when -- my shoulder as well, this ribbon, so that somebody wouldn't kill me from amongst our fighters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madame Judge, to avoid any mystification over the bands or ribbons, they were important so that on the battle front, Serb soldiers could be distinguished from the Muslim soldiers, because the uniforms might have been exactly the same, that was the only reason. And then the ribbons were changed, for example, "We're going into action today. We're going to have red ribbons, then blue, then yellow." So these ribbons would be changed so that they -- you could distinguish your own soldier and avoid friendly fire. From Vaske's unit, a soldier was killed in friendly fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, how do you know this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm an expert in military matters, Judge, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, truly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am noting that Mr. Seselj is testifying, basically. I would like you to ask the witness to put some letters on the picture. So now we only have circles. In a month or two, we won't know who's who, and maybe it would be useful to have letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have three circles on this picture. Witness, put a name -- Adil is the first one, so please put, yourself, the names of the people, and then a new number will be given to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks] [Interpretation] So that's right, you want the exact name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can write it down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's in blue, so we can't really read carefully. You can say it, and then we will compare it to the transcript. What is the first name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is "Sladjan Okilj" or whatever -- Okilj, anyway [indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okilj, Sladjan. Very well. The second name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zvonko Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zvonko Blazevic. Very well. And the third name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zekic, Zeko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zekic, Zeko. Very well. Can we please have a new number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the second annotated photograph will be Exhibit number C5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, can you see on this photograph that these soldiers are not all wearing the same uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That means that people wore what they found?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what they were given, what uniforms they were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And is this an M-84, the machine-gun called "Death sower," the one next-door to you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's your worst soldier, Jovan Colakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Come on, Mr. Sejdic, don't talk that way. They're your friends here.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're not my friends, Mr. Seselj. As far as I know, I was beaten most by this man and he threatened me most, and he put the rifle in my hand to have the photograph taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So that the Muslim authorities could persecute you afterwards?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, maybe that was the case.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You're telling the truth and I'm lying. Anyway, you were a member of the Work Platoon as well when you were taken on this photograph here?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that Work Platoon of yours numbered 25 men, as far as I remember. Right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So why did they select you from this whole Work Platoon to have your picture taken with them?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called me to the Command to load up the ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But why did they ask you to join them in having their photograph taken and give you a rifle?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you ask your man Jovan Colakovic why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because, Mr. Sejdic, I've already asked him, because everybody liked you in the unit, and soon after that you became a member of the unit?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say they liked me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then why did they mistreat me and beat me and threaten to rape my wife and kill my children?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nobody mistreated you, nobody beat you, and nobody threatened you. You've invented all that to justify, before the Muslim authorities, your participation in the war on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. Had they liked me, they would have let me go, together with my Muslims, but they held me prisoner for all those years and mistreated and tortured me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But as you say, your Muslims sent you away from Korita?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you don't keep saying "your Muslims." I was a Roma, belonged to the Roma ethnicity, the Roma population, and the Roma were not involved in the war at all. And if you asked us, we didn't have our state, we didn't have our representative, we didn't have anybody to lead us. We were slaves from times immemorial, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serbs were the only people in the whole of the Balkans who were friendly towards the Roma and never persecuted them; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yeah, because when it was World War II, Hitler persecuted the Serbs and the Jews all in one whole, so -- and gypsies were added here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we never persecuted the Roma or the gypsies, as you call them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down. It is impossible to translate at this speed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. The interpreters are having trouble following you. You are going too fast. Regarding this problem that the Chamber is hearing about, the Roma or Muslims, before the war, before 1991-1992, did you ever feel that you were discriminated by someone, as a Roma?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when I went to school, the children always called me "Gypsy, Roma." My faith cannot be different. I am the person who I am. I follow my faith and I live with my faith, just like everybody else, so I lived the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, religion-wise, and you don't have to answer this question if you don't want to - I'm only asking this as an information - do you have a religion or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm of the Muslim faith. "Safet" is my name. It's a Muslim name that my great-grandfather had and my grandfather. I don't know -- this has been the case since time immemorial. I don't know it was 50 or 70 or 100 years ago, we were all over the world, we the Roma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in the former Yugoslavia, all Romas, were they like you, of Muslim faith, or were there any Romas who were Catholics or Orthodox, or were you mainly of Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we're not all Muslims. The there are some of us who are Catholics and Serbs and Jews and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, where did you attend elementary school?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Semizovac, the Ribar Brothers was the name of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see. Since you had these problems before the war because of your ethnicity, were you ever in a position to have to declare yourself as a Bosniak as well?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you come up with questions like that. First you listen to all of this about my previous life, and now you come up with this, that the Muslims hated me, attacked me, whatever, this and that. I stated this, what I did; that is to say, that if I belonged to the Roma population, I could not have been a different person. I am the person I am, and I will remain the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to answer my question. Since you were not coerced, did you feel a need to declare yourself as a Bosniak by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What else can I be but a Bosniak? What else can I be if I'm called "Safet Sejdic"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Wait a second. Nowadays, the Bosniaks are the Bosnian Muslims who are of Serb origin, but of Muslim faith. But you're a Roma by ethnicity. You're not a Serb, you're not a Croat or a Bosniak. You're a Roma; right? The Roma are a reputable ethnicity that was seriously persecuted throughout history, but they also gave a considerable contribution to European culture. There is not a single European culture that the Roma did not contribute to.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Judge, I think that I pointed out a few moments ago in relation to the question that he's putting now. If I said that I'm a Roma by ethnicity, my grandfather, my great-grandfather, rather -- I don't even know, I wasn't even born then, they were under the authority of the Muslim people, they were under the authority of the Serb people. Then they would be Serbs. If did they were under the authority of the Croats, they would have been Croats. So I'm saying the way we were, and then I said what my grandfather's last name is, so I bear that last name, as my father does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, please be so kind as to answer my questions. I'm not challenging that your father was an honourable man, that your grandfather was an honourable man. All of that is well and fine. I'm asking you: How come that you were in a position a few years after the war to declare yourself as a Bosniak by ethnicity, that is to say, to push aside the fact that you're a Roma? And I think that there is nothing bad about that, a person being a Roma, just if he's a good and honourable man. Why did you push that aside and why did you declare yourself as a Bosniak? Why did you have to do that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because all the Roma predominantly in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- well, I mean, we've already discussed this. Some were Serbs and some were Croats and some were Jews and some were Muslims, some were Serbs. I've already answered this question. I've said that my population at that time was the way it was, and that's the way things remained. We -- I mean, my family -- how shall I put this? The so-called gypsies, we had to do what the other Muslims did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you have to declare yourself as a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I'm a Bosniak, then I'm a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you have to declare yourself to be one?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had to. I'm a Bosniak, and I remain a Bosniak. I'm a Muslim, and I remain a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was put to the witness in a repetitive way. The witness already explained to us that he's a Roma of Muslim faith, and I object that the same question be put to the witness over and over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I'm not mistaken, you said that your grandfather was Muslim. What is interesting is to see if originally your family, and tell us if you do know -- has your family always been in that region or area of the world or did it come from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, my family lived in that village, Svrake, and in the village of Semizovac for years. I was born in 1969. My grandfather and my relatives, of course, they were born before, that is, before I was born. They were always under Muslim authority, and they had Muslim names and surnames, and that's the way things remain to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, but going back in time, the 19th century, 18th century, 17th century, was your family always there or did they come from somewhere else? Of course, tell us only if you know it. You may not know your family tree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know exactly about that, because at that time I wasn't even born, you see. But when I listened to what my father had to say, and my grandfather, they say that officially our origins are in India.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So basically you would be originally from India. All right. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness confirmed for me here what it was that I had insisted upon. After the war, he was in a position to declare himself as a Bosniak, although he cannot be an ethnic Bosniak. He's a Roma. What I thought was necessary was to show how he was discriminated against, along ethnic lines, after the Dayton Agreement. That was the core of my question. Why would he declare himself as belonging to a different ethnic group rather than what his grandfathers had been for centuries? This Bosniak ethnicity has not been in existence ever, whereas the Roma have been in existence for centuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: I have a question to ask the witness on this. Witness, please, as far as you know, are there people of Serb ethnicity, of Croatian ethnicity, who lived in Bosnia after the war and declared themselves Bosnian -- Bosniak, in the B/C/S meaning of the word, "Bosniak" in B/C/S, because in French it would be what we call "Bosnien" which is Bosniak in English, so were there any people of Serb or Croat ethnicity who declared themselves "Bosnjaci"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean those who were Croats or Serbs after the war, that they were Bosniaks then, that they became Bosniaks, you mean? Could this please be interpreted for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let's try and clarify this, because it's complicated, because we have problems with translation of different concepts. For the Judges of the Bench, those we call "Bosnian," in French "Bosniak," are people of Muslim faith, and those which we call "Bosnian" in French or "Bosniak" in English, are those who have -- are citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, you can be a Bosniak, while you're Catholic, Orthodox or whatever, but when you're a Bosnian, it means that you're of Muslim faith. This is the parameters of the question. So what do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is to say that the Muslims call themselves the Bosniaks, and the Croats and the Serbs call themselves -- well, I mean, if it's "Bosniak," I mean, of Croatian nationality, then he belonged to Croatia. If it's a Serb, then he belonged to Serbia. So that was it, that is what they were called. But if they lived in Bosnia, I mean there, then they call them "Bosniaks" from time to time as well because they are the mainstay of that state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since obviously this topic is complicated for you regarding the national and ethnic question, Mr. Sejdic, a few moments ago in cross-examination you said that you did not know this name nicknamed Kele, Dragan Galic, whereas he claims that you slept on two adjacent beds in the dormitory of the Intervention Battalion. Do you still stand by this, that you don't know this Kele?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Sejdic, that's well and fine that you stand by that. Could we now display the statement given by this witness to the OTP in 2006. It is page 28, paragraph 112. Are you in a position to do that? I hope the Trial Chamber at least has this statement. If you have it, we don't have to put it on the ELMO, the statement from 2006? You say here: "Together with me in the Intervention Battalion were Makso Nikolic from Semizovac; Buco from Serbia, who was Rajko Koprivica's son-in-law or brother-in-law; Peka, the former mailman in Semizovac; Zvonko Blazevic, an ethnic Croat." That's the Zvonko you showed a few moments ago who got killed as well; right? Zvonko Blazevic, did he get killed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "... Sladjan Stevanovic from Semizovac; a certain Kele from Visoko; and Ranko Simic, commander of the platoon." In your statement, you refer to this Kele from Visoko, and now you don't remember at all -- you do not remember Kele at all, and you stand by that. So in 2006, you did remember Kele, and that's what you said to the investigators, and now all of a sudden you no longer remember Kele. Have you found it? It is page 28, paragraph 112. You have to take my document, then. Well, there you go. If the OTP doesn't want to do their own work, then -- 112 is the number of the paragraph. The OTP really had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you chose to defend yourself, so you have to do all the work. It's not the OTP that's supposed to do it. If you had counsel, he would be doing the work for you, but unfortunately as things stand now, you were supposed to do the work yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you suggesting to me that I find myself a lawyer who would defend me better than I'm defending myself, Madame Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Seselj. You are entitled to do so, but you must exercise this right in the best fashion possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madame Judge, I do my best, and I'm not successful in what I'm doing my best in. But if you have in mind a capable lawyer who would defend me better than I am defending myself, I would gladly look into your proposal or suggestion. All right. Have we got it on our screens now, the one-but-last line?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A certain Kele from Visoko, you identified him as a member of this Intervention Platoon, and now you don't remember him; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it's a different Kele.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was just one Kele?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there's just one Kele, then that's the Kele. But you said that he slept with me, that he knew everything about me. How would he not know if he was in the Intervention Platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, I did not say that he slept with you. I said that you slept on adjacent beds in the dormitory of the Intervention Platoon, and it was Kele who came from Visoko to Semizovac as a refugee on the 17th of July, 1992, and in 1993, he became a member of the Intervention Platoon, where you were one of the most prominent soldiers. That is what he says in his own statement, and you are saying that you don't know him at all, and now you recognised him. Thank you, thank you, so that we don't spend more time on this. Thank you for having recognised him.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing, Mr. Seselj. This Kele that you claim I slept with, I mean, one bed next to the other. See what you know. You are so pleased because you think that it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, it's not correct. I accept what you're saying, that it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And these statements, I don't know, on the basis of these statements of mine, you've got these statements, and now, by way of cross-examination through these statements, you are trying to put in all sorts of stories, hearsay, this and that. And where are all these people? Why were they not arrested? If they committed these atrocities, why weren't they arrested? What kind of information are you getting? People were saying Karadzic cannot be arrested, Mladic cannot be arrested. You are the one who knows everything. Why were they not arrested?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I know everything about them, but I would rather lose my own life than help anyone capture Karadzic or Mladic.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could before this Court, and if my authorities would let me, but I would be willing to lay my own life down in order to have you put away.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well and fine. Judges, you are listening to this, and you hear this witness threatening my life, and you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, listen you, too. I came here to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You came here to testify. The procedure is as such: The OTP calls witnesses, asks questions to these witnesses, and the accused is also entitled to ask questions to the witness. If Judges were managing everything from beginning to end, this would not occur in such a way. But the Judges who devised this Tribunal decided to opt for this solution, which is why we have to follow the rule, even -- that's just the rule. We have to play by it. Mr. Seselj is entitled to ask questions of you, and you are supposed to answer these questions. That's the rule of the game. We cannot do anything about it. And during cross-examination, he's entitled to put questions to you, so please put your feelings aside and just answer questions. Mr. Seselj, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, I'm a little frightened now. I'm worried that you might not kill me -- actually kill me, so my voice might tremble from time to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, this was useless, totally useless. You're just adding to the problem. Please proceed. Put questions and refrain from these type of comments, because this is only going to irk the witness and make him react. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If I don't even have the right to be afraid, what can I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, we have observed that in this elite unit, the Intervention Platoon of the Semizovac Battalion, there are at least three men who weren't Serbs by ethnicity; you, a Roma, and two Croats. Right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: One of the Croats was killed as a Serb fighter. That was Zvonko Blazevic. And another Croat is now living in Split, and he came to Belgrade to give me a statement. His name is Ninoslav Kaurinovic. That, nonetheless, testifies to the fact that there wasn't any ethnic intolerance in the Serb Army. The Serb Army fought for Republika Srpska against the rift in Yugoslavia, but there was no ethnic intolerance?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judges, I apologise. Now, can I ask a question? What were the Croats and the Serbs? Did they have the same cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, let's leave this matter of the crosses aside. We're not going to debate that point.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you say that the two of them -- that everybody was the same, not everybody could have been the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, do you know that in the Intervention Platoon of Vaske Vidovic from Ilijas, throughout the war there were two Muslims all the time? Did you ever hear about that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you believe me when I tell you that there were two Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they were there, I wasn't in Vaske's unit to know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But do you think I'm lying when I say that now?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not going to discuss that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me show you, Mr. Sejdic. I have here the original notebooks of Vaske's platoon. Now, could you display this page? We've already had it shown in court here, a photocopy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document has already been used. Maybe you were not in the courtroom at the time, but we've already seen this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number is 37 and 38. It says Mujo Djafic and Fadil Djafic. Show that to the witness, please. Yes, on the overhead projector. Do we see that on the ELMO? Do you see number 37 and 38, father and son, Mujo Djafic and Fadil Djafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I say I don't know about this, why are you showing it to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, just to see that I might not be lying this time.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they decided, they must have decided about this, just like for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, if I tell you, and I'm interested in your comment now, I put it to you and tell you that after the withdrawal of the Serb Army, Mujo and Faruk Djafic stayed on in Ilijas, that they were arrested by the Muslim authorities and beaten very brutally, and that Faruk Djafic, the son, that is, soon afterwards succumbed to the wounds he sustained during the beatings, and Mujo Djafic lived for a certain number of years and died recently, would you believe me?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not for Mujo or for this other man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, you're not. Now, madam, you can hand those original notebooks to the Trial Chamber. The Chetnik Vojvoda, Vasilije Vidovic, with expressions of deep respect, is donating that to you. They are the -- as the Trial Chamber, they are the work notebooks that you doubted existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. You're giving us these notebooks. The Trial Chamber should tender these as Court exhibits. Let me consult with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not proposing anything, Judges. You can receive that as a souvenir. You can give it to the Prosecutor to test its authenticity or do what you will with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless we have specific references, we cannot check whether we've already received a copy of these documents, and therefore I cannot make any submission as to their reliability and as to whether we object or not on their admission right here on the fly in the courtroom. We need time to check all this, and if we don't have the document, we need a copy of the document from Mr. Seselj in order to check things and in order to make an informed decision when the documents will be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if I remember well, the question already came up, and the Trial Chamber decided to answer negatively. I believe that we must first and foremost take a look at our prior decision in order to make sure that we do not issue a contradictory decision today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue with my cross-examination, since time is at a premium and I am afraid that you will deduct all this time from my time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we are not deducting this, but there is a problem. You are giving us six notebooks. Some of these notebooks are connected to Vaske Vidovic, because there are lists with mentions of his name. Furthermore, there are issues that might be of interest to the Trial Chamber; for example, the ethnical makeup of units in the VRS. You have just mentioned that there were two Muslim members, for example. Personally, I would admit these documents. However, if my colleagues disagree, we will not admit them. But we need to have a majority decision. I will consult with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. To solve this issue, the Trial Chamber is asking the Registrar to give it an MFI number. And if the person who, quote/unquote, is giving us these documents comes to testify, we will give it a real number, a final number. So please, Mr. Registrar, give us a number for these six notebooks, MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one number for all six.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be MFI C6.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, on my left, my case manager is telling me that we've never seen this document. Could we please have a copy, when we finally decide on admissibility, so that we can have a useful discussion, an informed discussion? We need to see a copy of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, can I ask you a question? You offered these notebooks to the Chamber, so I suppose you would wish to have them admitted as your exhibit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm just here as a go-between. Chetnik Vojvoda Vaske Vidovic, with sincere greetings to the Trial Chamber, sent the original of his notebooks, which you received on time during Theunens' -- expert witness Theunens' testimony, in the form of a photocopy. It was translated into English. There was a doubt expressed here as to its authenticity. My wife brought it on Friday. The Detention Unit service gave them to me yesterday, and I'm just conveying this from my friend, Vaske Vidovic, as a go-between. I'm never going to ask any document be tendered into evidence as a Defence document, and I've stated that many times. You can do what you will with those notebooks. You can take them home as a souvenir, you can give them to the OTP, you can throw them in the wastepaper basket, but I can't take them back again, I can't send them back again. I really can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This document will be MFI C6. I will ask the Registrar to make a copy of this document so that it can be handed out to the OTP, which may need it. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Towards the end of the examination-in-chief, Mr. Sejdic, you spoke about the preparation of the Serb units for an attack on the Niksic plateau, and you called that plateau the Crna Rijeka Plateau not the Niksic Plateau because there's a river there called Crna Rijeka; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Whereas it's the Niksic plateau?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Crna Rijeka, Niksic Plateau, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right. And you said that the attack began at the end of 1993 or the beginning of 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I came by a precise piece of information which tells me that the attack was launched on the 8th of November, 1993. And when I present that information to you, when I tell you that, do you consider that that is correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what information you received. I know what I said in my statement. Now, your statements, well, I don't know whether they're correct or not, because you receive them from lists, from Vaske, et cetera, and you bring them in here as a souvenir. And you know what a souvenir means. A souvenir is given to the Muslims, and not everybody is a Muslim in the courtroom here, when you talk about souvenirs, when you say, "Vaske sent souvenirs." All of these statements of yours, using the "tu" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You keep addressing me in the singular, "tu," and that is beginning to upset me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, why are you so informal? You are being aggressive in doing so. You are a witness of justice. You're not supposed to use "tu," the informal way of addressing Mr. Seselj. You should use a formal way of addressing him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Judge. Perhaps it just came out of my lips. But he addresses me in all kinds of ways and he's laughing at me, and I have to take all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you believe that the accused is being provocative by smiling at you, just don't watch him, don't look at him. Look at the Bench and just answer the question. Keep cool, please. There's no need to get all worked up. Please stay cool. It might be difficult, but please try to do so. Let's come back to the Niksic Plateau. Mr. Seselj, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, I do have to try and convince you that I'm not laughing at you, and if I happen to have a smile on my face, it's an expression of sympathy, because I do sympathise with your bad fate after 1996. However, if you consider this to be that I'm laughing at you, I'm sorry for that. You, using the "tu," would like to see me hang from a branch somewhere; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would like you to have left with the Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then you wouldn't have had to undergo all the suffering. But I ask you, once again, not to use the "tu." I really find that irritating. Perhaps I have high opinions of myself, but it is a bit irritating to me when someone keeps addressing me in the familiar form of "tu."

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Seselj, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now you said that this was at the end of 1993 to 1994. That is a time-frame, a period of time. Now, I looked into this and established when the attack on the Niksic Plateau was, and I came to see that it was on the 8th of November. Do you deny that it was the end of November? The 8th of November is indeed the end of 1993. So it's not in my interests that it should be closer to the indictment period, it would be in my interest that it was in 1994, whereas it was on the 8th of November, 1993. Do you consider that that is not correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that it was correct or incorrect. In my statement, it says, and I stressed, either the end of 1993 or the beginning of 1994, because I can't remember exactly, but that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, that is not contained in any of your statements, and I have a total of five statements of yours, two which you gave to the Muslim authorities in 1996 and then to The Hague investigators. I think that was in 1996, too. Then the investigators again in 2004, and then The Hague investigators in 2006. And never did you mention this rallying of the Serb Army prior to the attack on the Niksic Plateau at which Radovan Karadzic -- Karadzic, Mladic and I were there, myself. You never said that. You said that during the examination-in-chief here in court first. Why?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I recognised you, "tu," and I because I didn't remember to emphasise that when you were there and when I saw you because there was no talk about you, "tu," and I didn't know that I would be with you, "vous," or, rather, "tu" here in the courtroom. And when I was on the plateau, the Niksic Plateau, when Dragan Josipovic and Jankovic and Vaske were discussed, and when they came to that attack, I happened to see you, "tu," as I told you the first day in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has now addressed me nine times in the familiar form of "tu," the second-person singular, nine times during what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, maybe every day in your language when you speak, in everyday language, you always use the informal way of addressing people. Maybe to you, using "tu," the informal way, is commonplace. Is that the problem, that you say "tu" to everyone? Mr. Seselj, then don't get all worked up. If he addresses you in such an informal way, it's his way of speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. President. First of all, I'm not taking offence at all. If you accept this explanation, that this is the customary way in which the witness speaks, then I'm not going to intervene any longer. See how constructive I am? I relent straight away. Truth to tell, you did frighten me with a few of your interventions, so I'm more amenable than usually. But what can a person do? In the later years of one's life, one does get to feel weaker, doesn't one. I identified the date as the 8th of November. The Prosecution can check that, because -- well, the date is the 9th of November, and I was helped out there by General Dragan Josipovic, who gave me his statement, and we're going to look through that statement now, as a statement by Vasilije Vidovic, who had taken part in the attack on the Niksic Plateau. Just now, with the assistance of my associates, I looked this up and found out what it was that I did on the 9th and 10th and the 11th of November, 1993, so could we please have document number 9, Roman numeral IX on the overhead projector. This is my book, "Rule the Roost," "Dedinje Dizdar." This is the amended edition from 2002. The cover page can be seen on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And now could you have a look at the following. There is an interview of mine, entitled "Serbian Money in Cyprus." On the 9th of November, 1993, obviously, I was a guest speaker at Radio Stara Pazova. Can you see that, Mr. Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not interested in this paper at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Next page, please. On the 10th of November, I spoke at Radio Sabac, and that is where I gave an interview that was entitled "Machine-gun Nests Defend the House of Flowers." Next page. On the 10th of November, I was also in Loznica. So I had two radio interviews, in actual fact. I gave an interview that was entitled "Drina: The Drina River Will Not Be a Border," as it won't. And on the 11th of November, I gave an interview to Radio Temerin, entitled "The Government of the Financial State Mafia." At that time, there was an election campaign going on in Serbia in 1993, and every day I was a guest speaker on radio or TV throughout Serbia, and it never crossed my mind to travel to Republika Srpska, as the campaign was in full sway. On the 15th of September, we started toppling the Milosevic government, headed by Nikola Sainovic, and after a long debate in Parliament that went on for three or four weeks, Slobodan Milosevic dissolved the National Assembly and we had early elections. I did not move out of Serbia on all of those until the election campaign was over in December. Do you believe that, Mr. Sejdic, when I say that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How did you find all these excuses, and you went to speak to your Serbs and support them, and now you're trying to say that you did not go to the Crna Rijeka Plateau as well? You didn't have a helicopter, you had nothing, right, nothing to bring you there, at least for an hour, half an hour, and then leave, and attend these governments and what have you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you swore under oath that you had seen Mr. Seselj on that plateau. This is what you told us. Mr. Seselj is now bringing some documents, showing you some documents, establishing that on the 8th, 9th and 10th of November, he was giving interviews here and there. Of course, you're saying that with the helicopter, one can come on the plateau, stay half an hour, one hour, and then leave again and give an interview, of course, but the problem is the following: If Mr. Seselj is showing that he was not there, in his mind, he never came there, but, on the other hand, you state that you saw him. This is where the debate lies. So please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was in Vogosca, Ilijas and Ilidza, the first time in 1994 and the second time in 1994. But in 1993, I did not go to that area at all. In November 1993, the attack at the Niksic Plateau started, and in 1994, when I came to the part of the Niksic Plateau facing the Olovo frontline, that was sometime in the spring of 1994. I toured the positions at the frontline, and there was no fighting going on then. Otherwise, at the Niksic Plateau we had a group of volunteers from Serbia, a group of volunteers from the Serb Radical Party. However, they were not moving from Ilijas and Vogosca, but from the completely opposite direction. Olovo was in Muslim hands, and the villages above Olovo were in Serb hands. I just wanted to explain a few things to you, if you're interested. This can even be calculated as my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the accused can put documents to the witness, put questions to the witness, but now he's testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can do the same thing by putting questions, rather than testifying. He is making a statement right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you heard Mr. Seselj say that the first time he went there was in 1994, so what do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned that in my statements, that is to say, the end of 1993, the beginning of 1994, so that's it. Secondly, his paramilitary units, that is to say, the mercenaries, Seselj's mercenaries, they arrived just before the attack was to start. They arrived during the night, and I pointed that out in my statements. They arrived on seven buses in the school in Semizovac, and in front of the Kulin Dvor command at Ranko Jankovic's, and that's when these units went to the Crna Rijeka village. They attacked it, actually. So they were getting off trucks, and they wore yellow ribbons or armbands.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, it is important for the Prosecutor to find where it was that the witness stated this earlier on, because the statements that I have do not contain this about these seven buses. Should I continue with my questions now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1994, when I arrived in Vogosca, I was at Ilijas and Ilidza. General Josipovic, he was a colonel then, he toured the Serb positions at Zuc together with me. Your unit was there, too; right? Isn't that right, Mr. Sejdic, it was at Zuc?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that you shook hands with me on that occasion, Mr. Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You forgot that as well?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Over the weekend, I consulted my friend Radovan Karadzic, and I asked him where he was on the 9th of November, 1993. And Radovan Karadzic informed me that on the 9th of November, he was in Belgrade, and that there he gave an interview to TV Reuters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're giving us a scoop. You're telling us that during the weekend, you saw Mr. Radovan Karadzic, who is wanted by the entire world. Should we understand it that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add the following --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not see him. I was in contact with him through an intermediary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, because the sentence, as it is drafted in English on line 17, page 85, it says: "I consulted my friend," so we were under the impression that you had a connection with him. But now you're telling us that it was by other intermediaries?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... that we were in contact, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if we should give credit as to what is said, it should be told clearly, how the contact took place. I would be very happy if Mr. Seselj would -- were able to shed some light on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, allow him to finish his question. Mr. Seselj, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would provide that information, Judge, but I don't want it to be taken up as my time. I will tell you in great detail how it was that I contacted Radovan Karadzic, but I don't want that to be included in my time. So do you insist on this or not? If not -- well, the Prosecutor insists. I don't know if you insist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will consult my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber will not subtract this from your time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I instructed my associates to contact certain individuals who are in contact with Radovan Karadzic. I asked them to provide me with information as to where Radovan Karadzic was on the 9th of November. I received information that Radovan Karadzic was in Belgrade, and I thank my friend Radovan Karadzic for having kindly sent me this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please put your question to the witness, then, since on the 9th of November, Mr. Karadzic was not on the plateau.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since it was not possible for me to take a statement from Radovan Karadzic, because I don't know who could certify that statement, I instructed my legal associates to look up, in the daily press, possible traces of Radovan Karadzic's stay in Belgrade, and they found these traces for me. And here it is on page 6 of document number 9. You have a photocopy from the newspaper "Borba," dated the 10th of November, that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you have an article stating that in Belgrade, Radovan Karadzic, on the previous day in an interview with TV Reuters, said the Serbs are ready to make territorial concessions. Do you see that? So Radovan Karadzic, on the 9th of November, could not have been at the Niksic Plateau and in Belgrade; right? Isn't that right, Mr. Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I think all of these things that you said about Karadzic, all of these are tricks and lies on your part. So you can hang that around your neck so that you do not forget this as you walk in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we've already stated that I'm not just an ordinary liar, but the greatest liar in this courtroom, but I still have to go on putting my questions to you, although I'm a liar. So try to endure this.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm patient enough as it is. I was so patient after all those years of your provocations. But you saying that you shook hands with me at Zuc, I mean, I would rather shake hands with a rock or a tree than with you, even if I were to get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I know that when you fell under the Muslim rule, you regretted the fact that you shook hands, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have on the ELMO a paper dated 10th of November, 1993, and it talks about the presence of Mr. Karadzic, who was giving an interview to Reuters, and this would be on the 9th of November. So this is a strong element. What do you have to say to this, independently of the fact that there is a certain amount of antagonism between you and Mr. Seselj ? That does not concern us, but we would like to know if what you said is true or, rather, that you, yourself, saw Karadzic, Mladic and Mr. Seselj on that plateau while a combat operation was taking place, and this is what you told us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what I claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So this is what you confirm to us, but we have to establish on what date did you see all this. It would appear that the combat operation took place in the month of November, but in November, Mr. Seselj was elsewhere. Mr. Karadzic was in Belgrade, and that is a problem. How do you resolve -- how do you solve, correction, this problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, Your Honour, this problem ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you cannot answer. Very well. For the Trial Chamber, I would like to mention that this article can place Karadzic somewhere on the 9th of November, but the interview that he gave, it could also have been done by phone or otherwise. It doesn't necessarily mean that he had to be present in Belgrade. This is what the Trial Chamber may note. I'm just saying this, but please proceed. I see that the time is ticking, so we might not be able to finish this witness today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I don't know how a television interview can be given over the telephone, but I'm going to put the following question to the witness:

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Karadzic said, and this is on the same page, but in the second paragraph: "We are prepared to talk and re-examine the possibility of making some territorial concessions to the Muslims, especially in Sarajevo." Said Radovan Karadzic in his interview to Reuters Television in Belgrade. And then the quotation continues: "We continue to advocate the continuation of talks, and we are prepared to help the Muslims get a larger part of Sarajevo and some other territories," added Karadzic. Now please look at page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, while the page is being put on the ELMO, I would like to note that I did not get these documents prior to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had this photocopied before the cross-examination. Now, why the Prosecutor didn't get a copy or why he lost his copy, I don't know. But, at any rate, he certainly received a copy of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, this document apparently was sent to you at 7.41 this morning, or arrived at 7.41, correction. When Mr. Seselj got it, he gave to the Registry photocopies, and I met them at 8.20 and the Registrar told me that there were some documents.
