utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just notice that all these documents were stapled together, so in fact I was not able to find it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 8 of the document that is under Roman numeral IX. It is very clear, and it's very easy to find. What we see here is a photocopy of the newspaper called "Vecernje Novosti," dated the 10th of November. They carried a similar article. Dr. Radovan Karadzic says Bosnian Serbs are prepared to make concessions. In paragraph 2, it also says: "Karadzic said the following in his interview to TV Reuters in Belgrade." Mr. Sejdic, do you think both Karadzic and I were both at the Niksic Plateau and then took a helicopter and went to Belgrade; is that possible?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but you have all the resources one could think of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned helicopters a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said "maybe by helicopter," I think that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that at the end of 1993, NATO air forces had controlled the airspace above Bosnia-Herzegovina and not a single aeroplane was able to take off without agreement from them?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Keep that to yourself. As far as I know, you had all the resources at your disposal. Whatever you wanted to do, you could have done. NATO has been looking for Karadzic and Mladic for ages and can't find him. He's in Belgrade, Zagreb, Serbia, wherever, now he's here, then he's there, but you had the resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I tried to receive similar information from my friend Ratko Mladic, but they're going to be one or two days late, so I won't be able to use that information in this particular cross-examination, but never mind, perhaps it's not essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have to take a break now. We're going to take a 20-minute break, and we will resume at 10 to 12.00. And, of course, the hearing will finish at 1.15. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The question is way too personal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I anticipated that already, so I ordered a redaction. We will resume at 10 after 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Registrar, please, could you move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to respond to this assertion made by counsel for the Prosecution. According to 65 ter, the material was submitted to me only in October last year, and on the 6th of November, the trial started -- rather, the 7th of November. It was the pre-trial conference that was held on the 6th. And I quite literally prepare for every witness that is to come. I don't have time to prepare for several witnesses at the same time. As they announce that a particular witness will come, that is how I carry out my preparation. When they make the wrong announcement, as was often the case until now, then I prepare for the wrong person. They announced Ivan Grujic, and I prepared for him, and I was snowed under with all these autopsy findings, and lo and behold, they gave up on him, they're not going to bring him at all, and now all of a sudden they're going to bring some colleague of his from work, a lady. I did not have enough time to prepare for these witnesses. Until October 1996, I did not have material from the OTP. For five years, they hoped that I would have an attorney imposed upon me and that they would be able to put in whatever they wanted to. They would have a passive defence, gung-ho, they would insert whatever they wanted to, and that would be it. So, anyway, I am going to continue preparing for each and every witness only when a particular witness is announced, and the Prosecution will have to face the facts; namely, that documents arrive only later. Now I received a document because my associates realised that we were disputing the date of the death of Sladjan Okilj, so can we have this document that I received just now placed on the ELMO and I'm going to put a question to the witness. I have no other way to clarify the dates, and the Prosecution did not carry out the investigation properly. Had they done it properly, they would have given us a review of all dates, they would have said the attack on the Niksic Plateau started on such-and-such a date and so on and so forth. There was no investigation, so now I have to conduct the investigation. So this is a book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is the book, "The Nemanjics of Ilijas." The author is Velemir Adzic, and we showed this when (redacted). So please go all the way to page 144. It is page 5 here for us, so that the witness can see there is a list here of the Serbs who got killed during this war. And under number 342 is the name of Sladjan Okilj, father's name Nikola, member of the Reconnaissance Platoon of the 5th Infantry Battalion, born on the 19th of April, 1974, in Vares; got killed on the 23rd of October, 1993, in the village of Vis, Zuc, near Vogosca, by a hand grenade that was thrown by the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Prosecutor is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name of a witness was mentioned, and I would like a redaction because this witness had been granted protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I won't say anything because we're not in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can remember he testified in public. If I've made a mistake, I truly am sorry. The name can be redacted, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we in private session, Mr. -- sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, line 10, page 104, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's exactly it, he had protective measures. I would like a redaction. I would like Mr. Seselj to make sure in the future to check things before he actually mentions names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, this witness had been granted protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I truly am sorry. My mistake. Once again, I'm going to read this out or, rather, I'm going to say -- I mean, with my -- I mean, giving my consent that this be redacted, the book that I'm quoting is "The Nemanjics of Ilijas," written by Velemir Adzic, and on page 144, under number 342, among the casualties from Ilijas and Vogosca, under number 342 there's a reference to Sladjan Okilj, father's name Nikola, member of the Reconnaissance Platoon of the 5th Infantry Battalion, born on the 19th of April, 1974, in Vares; got killed on the 23rd of October, 1993, in the village of Vis, Zuc, near Vogosca; was killed by a hand grenade that had been thrown by the enemy. He was buried at the Ljubina-Semizovac Cemetery."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you. No need to dwell on this document any further. Now, I have obtained a few more statements by persons whom you know from this war, so, first of all, we are going to have a look at Roman numeral I. That's the number of the statement, the statement of Vasilije Vidovic. And now I'm going to indicate certain sections of this statement to you, and you are going to tell me whether that is true or not. His statement was compiled on the basis of your statement and on the basis of your examination-in-chief. Could you please take this and put it on the overhead projector. Roman numeral I is the number of the statement. First of all, Vasilije Vidovic here denies that he took part in the fighting in the village of Svrake at all. Although you did not say that in your previous statements, on one occasion you did say that he took part in that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vaske Vidovic took part in the beginning when the mosque was destroyed. That's when he came with his artillery and he destroyed the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1992 to 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: End of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: End of 1992, I mean?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Or the beginning of 1993. Were there any Muslims in the village of Svrake then?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't that many Muslims left then, because the Muslims were taken away by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's see what Vasilije Vidovic says: "My unit and I, as its commander, never took part in any fighting for the village of Svrake. Throughout the war in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, I and none of my soldiers ever entered this village. The village of Svrake was in the rear. We only passed by it when we went to the frontline. To this day, I do not know, as I did not know then, what happened in that village. When I returned from medical treatment in mid-May, 1992, I spent some time in Ilijas, where there was no fighting. The first fighting that I took part in with my unit took place near Podlugovo [as interpreted], where the Muslim forces were advancing from the direction of Breza." Is this correct, is this true, what Vasilije Vidovic is saying?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. He says further on: "I and the other members of my unit were never called 'Seselj's men' by anyone, nor could I interpret that nickname. People called the soldiers from my unit 'Vaske's Chetniks,' from the very first fight that we took part in." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they could not have called Vaske as a man of Seselj's. I remember mentioning him as a local man. The mercenaries, Seselj's men, came and joined him at the frontline and the fighting that he took part in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did these mercenaries belong to his unit?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On that list of members of his unit, can you identify the mercenaries who is not from that area?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, because people knew -- I mean, I would distinguish them on the basis of their uniforms, insignia, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Further on, Vidovic says: "I have never heard of the existence of this so-called Planja's house. I do not know at all where it is or what it looks like. Also, throughout the war I never had any deputy in the unit."

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. And now is this true? Vasilije Vidovic says: "I never entered, during the course of the war, any tyre repair shop in Vogosca, and in particular, I did not run this kind of a store. I note that Vogosca and Ilijas are two different municipalities, in terms of military and civilian organisation, and since I and my unit belonged to Ilijas only, even if I wanted to, I could not have been given any shop from the territory of a different municipality."

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. Vasilije Vidovic could have run whoever or whatever he wanted, because that is how Josipovic rewarded him. Vidovic knew of Planja's house, the garage, everything else. I think that I have already mentioned all of that. This is correct, it is contained in my statements. And if it is not correct, you can ask the Muslim people, who were in the prisons, whether they knew Vaske.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Vaske Vidovic says: "The officer who was my direct superior was General Dragan Josipovic. He was commander of the Tactical Group, commanded the brigades from Ilijas, Ilidza, Rajlovac, and Vogosca." Not only the brigade of Vogosca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned in my statement that the commander of the battalion was Dragan Josipovic, near Vogosca, [indiscernible], called "Sonja," that he was authorised in terms of all the axes, Ilijas, Vogosca, Semizovac and the other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, do you know what the difference is between a brigade and a battalion?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know that he was the top man then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, he was commander of the Tactical Group that included four brigades -- five brigades -- four brigades?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you know that it's four or five, it's got to be more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Four brigades.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly more than that, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Look at what Vasilije Vidovic says: "No one ever carried ammunition for my unit, because this was a mechanised unit. All the ammunition was on the vehicles."

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that I carried this ammunition for Vasilije Vidovic. It was for Rajko Jankovic and his combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did anybody else carry weapons for Vasilije Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Others from the work platoon should know that. If they carried this for Vaske, then they should know. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You did not hear of a work platoon being subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like I didn't hear of these two Muslims being on the frontline with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, as for the description you provide for Vaske Vidovic, this is what he says: "As for my personal weapons, I never carried a weapon with a short barrel. Rather, I carried a revolver only. I am not aware of any sabre. I could not enter a single vehicle from my unit with it. I never wore any kind of military overalls. On the traditional flag that we carried around, there weren't any crossed sabres. Rather, it was crossed bones that are in line with tradition." He is referring to Chetnik traditions here. Don't you know that no one ever saw Vaske Vidovic with this sabre that you refer to?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true, that is a lie. I know full well what it was that he carried and what I saw, and I stated that and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. What's the point of this sabre in wartime? What can one do with a sabre, except for the fact that it can only bother a man who had been wounded 13 times and who limped visibly?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you go ahead and ask him. If he wanted to slaughter someone, he would with that sabre. In Crna Rijeka, he slaughtered a man, a Muslim who was a driver, and he cut off his head and he put it on a pole, and then he said, "Finally I got rid of this man." I guess that he harmed him before the war, so he was pleased that he had cut off this man's head.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you see him cutting off this man's head?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him doing it, but I saw the head on the pole and I heard him say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you said, during the examination-in-chief, that he put it on the hood of his jeep?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, later on he put it on the hood of that jeep. When they were leaving Crna Rijeka, then he took the skull and he put it on his jeep so that he could brag as he passed through Semizovac and all the other villages, so that people could see what it was that Vaske Vidovic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he already had a skull on that jeep?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was an older skull. I don't know from what century.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know from what century that skull was? Could it have been a plastic skull, maybe?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, possibly. I did not get any closer to it, and I didn't caress it, certainly, but I saw that it was a skull.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I saw that skull, too, and I drove in Vaske's jeep.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what kind of a jeep was it? Was it enjoyable?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very enjoyable. There was a skull on the hood, and there was a helmet on it, too. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the helmet, but at any rate you enjoyed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's not talk about how I felt. How could you see the skull without seeing the helmet? All of Ilijas, all of Vogosca, all of Ilidza saw on the hood of Vaske's jeep a skull and a blue helmet of the UN.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that there was a helmet. There was only a skull.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Without a helmet?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without a helmet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: With my very own eyes, I saw a UN blue helmet.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you did, Mr. Seselj, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So in addition to this skull, how could you affix the head that had been cut off somebody's body?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a pole, where the flag was, the black flag that I've already described. It was on that pole that that head was fixed, and then he drove the jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And why, not in a single statement that you gave to The Hague Tribunal or the Muslim authorities, did you mention the fact that this head was placed on the jeep by Vaske Vidovic? That does not exist in any of your statements.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I said he placed it on a pole, and when the fighting was over in that area, he took the head and put it on his car and drove it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: My question to you is: Why, not in a single statement that you gave either to the Muslim authorities or The Hague investigators, did you say that Vaske Vidovic affixed a head that had been cut off to his jeep?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't exist in any of your statements.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Perhaps you said it. Perhaps this was highly unbelievable and they didn't want to put it in your statement. But let's see what Vaske Vidovic says with respect to that skull, and that is paragraph 2 on page 2 of his statement. He says: "The skull on the hood of my car was a plastic one, and it was brought to me by my friends from a school that had been destroyed. As far as I know, it was a secondary school of some sort in a place called Srednje." Was there a secondary school in a place called Srednje?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a school in Srednje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What secondary school was that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the name of the school exactly, but I do know that there was a school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it possible that in the biology laboratory, they might have had a plastic skull there in that school?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I be expected to know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you said that the skull was hundreds of years old, centuries old; right? Anyway, at -- in any case --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speculative questions are put to the witness. He cannot answer to this type of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, Mr. Seselj, proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, it's important for me to have heard that the witness said that the skull on the hood of the car was hundreds of years old. He can't know whether it was a real one or not. At first, when I saw it, I thought it was a real one, and then I asked around and I was told that it was plastic. When I saw the UN helmet, I found that rather nice, because it wasn't a threat to the Muslim civilians but a threat to the UN soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you mentioned the skull a moment ago, what I know is this: You asked how old was it -- how old it was, and I said I didn't know. I said perhaps from times immemorial, perhaps not. So you can't speak that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. We don't know the origins of the skull. Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know now. You're saying that instead of a real one, it might have been plastic, so that means that you know. You saw it, you saw the helmet. I did not see it. What I saw, I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I saw it, and Vaske Vidovic says that it was plastic, but it's immaterial whether it was an old real skull or a plastic one. I liked the way it was used as a threat to the UN, but we won't dwell on that point. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a threat to the UN. It was a threat to the Muslims so that they should know, when they see it, who Vaske Vidovic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these comments are completely inappropriate. Questions can be put, the witness can answer, but this is repetitive and that's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, your comment on that skull with regard to the UN is absolutely inappropriate. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, did you hear that at the beginning of the summer 19 -- that I was almost killed in the jeep where this plastic skull was with the UN helmet; did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was in the jeep, myself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had I heard that you'd been killed in the jeep, that would have made me very happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm going to tell you something now, and you confirm whether you know something about that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the interpreters were not able to catch the date. It was in the summer of 1993, I imagine, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1994, Mr. President, 1994. 1994 was the first time I was in Ilijas, and I was in the jeep. I'm providing this information to the witness. And then I asked him whether he had heard anything about that. On my way back from visiting Ilijas, Vogosca and Ilidza, I was also in Hadzici, anyway, I was in a jeep driven by Vaske Vidovic. I was in the front seat. Behind me were Tomislav Nikolic and Nikola Poplasen, and at the very back there was a soldier, and we were going across Poljine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where Poljine is?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's an elevation above Sarajevo where the Serbs had to make a new road in order to connect Ilijas, Vogosca and Ilidza with Pale; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Anyway, from the Muslim positions a Maljutka was fired. Do you know what weapon a Maljutka is?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have absolutely no idea. It's a mortar?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's a guided anti-aircraft missile. Anyway, that Maljutka missed our jeep by half a metre, and the news went 'round Vogosca straight away, in Ilijas, Hadzici, Vogosca, how we were targeted by a Maljutka and how we managed to escape, just.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I know about all that? You were driven there, driven back. You toured the lines. Who knows? You might have come across a tank mine, you might have come across a bomb. I know nothing about that. I didn't hear anything about that, and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you saw me at Zuc hill. You were deployed with your unit there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't repeat that. I said I hadn't seen you there, and I didn't shake your hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So I'm lying and you're telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say you were lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that I'm lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that particular point, Mr. Seselj, in 1994, apparently was in the area on board a vehicle, and some witness can confirm this. Mr. Nikolic would be one of them. And there was another person with him, Nikola Poplasen. If he is driving around and if he is in the area, he must have gone to meet the fighters, and a political figure, when he meets combatants, fighters, he will shake hands with them. So are you absolutely certain you did not meet him at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see him in the Zuc area at all, the fact that he says that I was at Zuc and he shook hands with me. No. The day that I said I saw him personally at the Crna Rijeka Plateau, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Mladic, Dragan Josipovic and the rest of his fighters and bodyguards, that's when I said I saw him, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, wouldn't it seem strange to you if I were to say that never during the war did I see General Ratko Mladic in the area of Republika Srpska? I just met him twice, both times in Belgrade and he was wearing civilian clothes. Do you believe me when I say that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A moment ago, as far as I remember it, before this statement, when I was saying that you were on the plateau, that Crna Rijeka Plateau, that you were with Karadzic and Mladic and the rest of them, when I said that, you said after 1994, that you did tour those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But I wasn't with them.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, you, "tu" were with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you don't believe me when I tell that I never met Ratko Mladic in Republika Srpska during the war?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I believe you? Why am I here? I'm here as a witness to testify about what I saw, and that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Well, I can confirm that you're a very honest witness here.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to take that, how to understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Inappropriate comments, Mr. President. Objection to these comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Vaske Vidovic goes on to say that on Zuc hill, there were never any houses. At the foot of the hill, all that existed was several Serb houses, and throughout the time people lived in those houses. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who lived in those houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Serbs were there, but in only some houses. Some houses were occupied lower down towards Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the Muslims weren't in that area at all at the foot of the hill?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the Muslims were up at the line, feature 850, elevation 850.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Muslim units?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at feature 850, and the Serbs were at feature 830.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the position of the Muslim units was 20 metres higher up than the Serb positions, at a higher altitude; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So elevation 850 is 850 metres above sea level. From the Muslim positions, and then 20 metres up, the Serb positions could be seen far better than could the Muslims from the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say. I didn't draw up any maps, or sketches, or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, explain to me what sort of human shield that the Serbs employed opposite the Muslim forces. What did this human shield or live wall look like? Human shield, I'm talking about, human shield.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the human shield was made up of Muslims from the work platoons who had been captured when they were taken to the container which was on the other side; that is to say, nearer to Zuc and the Muslim units than the other side towards Rajlovac and Serbia. So that's where the container was set up, in the Serb zone, and that's where the Muslims were incarcerated overnight. While they were digging and working, when the Muslims weren't shooting, they would let them dig. Now, after that, that is to say, when the attack on Zuc should have taken place and on these Muslims and the rest of us who were there, as I've already said, so that was the human shield. When the attack took place on Zuc, that's when they sent us into the frontlines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please, you have given me a long answer, but not answered my question. I still haven't been able to understand what this human shield looked like at Zuc. The Muslims were 20 metres higher up than the Serb positions. They were above the Serb positions. The work platoon took part in digging the trenches. That is what a labour platoon does. If you have to do labour, you dig trenches. Now, the prisoners weren't allowed to be in these work platoons. If the prisoners were brought in, then that was a crime. But you were in a work platoon and you weren't a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who asked anybody whether they were prisoners or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's not the essential part. You're working in a work platoon, and the work you were doing was digging trenches. That's clear to me. You were exposed to risk because the member of a work platoon can also be killed, and perhaps some of them were. But what did the human shield look like? Explain that to me. There are Serb trenches and there are Muslim trenches across the way. The Muslim trenches were 20 metres higher up, at an elevation 20 metres higher than the Serb positions. How, then, could the Serb soldiers use you, from the work platoon, as a human shield? I'm not clear on that, I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the line was falling and the Muslims tried to break through the frontline of the Serb Army, when there weren't enough people from the Serb Army up at the frontlines, and while the reinforcements were arriving, while we were escaping from the shooting, they made us go in front of them as a human shield.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How do you mean "in front of them"? If trenches exist, then the distance between trenches was 15 to 20 metres; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not 15 to 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how -- what was the distance?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Let's take the distance between the trenches of the two enemy sides to be 100 metres. The Muslims are on the attack. The Serbs feel that they have too few men, so what did they do then? They took you from the work platoon and place you in front of their lines, in front of their trenches, to protect themselves that way; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, very nicely. They put us in front, when they tried to push the trenches back. The Muslims had already taken two or three trenches. They tried to take them back. They couldn't do that, and then there was an all-out attack. It was a fierce attack from Zuc hill. That means that the Muslims attacked the Serb frontlines. However, they didn't have enough men, and they placed us there so that they could fight to take control of the line again. And as far as I remember, there was a statement given by Alija Izetbegovic to the fact that -- he was asked whether our men should hit the human shield or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Leave Izetbegovic alone. You still haven't explained to us what a human shield looks like. If the Muslims are on the attack, then the Serbs -- and the Serbs have few fighters and they need you to act as reinforcements, they have to provide you with weapons if you are going to be reinforcements, because if you're sitting in a trench without weapons, then that doesn't mean a thing.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They made us go in front. We were escaping but they made us move forward, and they went along behind us, shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no problem as to the question, but the question is repeated over and over. The witness answer what he could answer, but I would like to raise an objection because the question is being repeated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And slow down, please, because it is impossible to translate at this speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, don't put the question over and over, unless you really want to highlight another aspect of your question. But I don't see it, actually.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I seem to be the most stupid here. It seems that just -- it's just me that can't understand what this human shield looked like. I'm clear on the fact that the Muslims are attacking and that the Serbs have to defend themselves with very few men. I'm clear that the members of the work platoon are trying to escape. I understand that the army is trying to get them to come back to the trenches, or near the trenches, but how they place them forward as a human shield, I just don't understand that. And how is it possible to have that kind of human shield? Perhaps you understand this. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't understand more than you. Witness, you were there. This term "human shield" is used in this Tribunal quite often. At times, it refers to people digging holes, and at other times it refers to people who are acting as a human wall, under fire. So were you under fire, under Muslim fire, in order to protect the Serbs from the Muslim fire, or were you a human shield for something else? Because when we use this term, "human shield," it also presupposes that there's a creation of an obstacle perhaps for a bullet to go through, so it's a screen stopping bullets to go through. So would the Serbs put you between them and the Muslims so that you would get fired at first and killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the aim of preventing the Muslims to enter their territory. That's why they placed us there, for us to die and they to protect themselves and to shoot at the Muslims from behind our backs or in front of our chests, to shoot at them that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if the Muslims were attacking Serb positions, and you were there in the first lines without any weapons, it is obviously clear that you would get killed first, but this will not stop the Muslim forces from moving on, if they have the intention to take over the position. This is where I'm losing you. What is the purpose of creating a human shield unless it's just to kill people for fun? Please explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can explain that, Mr. President. That human shield was composed of us, the work platoon, and when the Serbs started placing us into this human shield and forcing us ahead, there was firing. When the shooting started, we were shot at from all sides. The Muslims at the time said they had come across a human shield and should not shoot, and there were public apologies. Several months later, I saw this on television when Alija spoke about it. So he said, "You have to shoot. Do not allow the Serbs to enter Sarajevo. If the Serbs were to enter Sarajevo, it would be the end of the world." So that's why they placed us there, and the Muslims and the Serbs had to shoot at us, and we were a human shield. That's what a human shield is. When the attack on Zuc was called, he knows what the attack on Zuc means and what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that you were positioned in such a way that both Muslims and Serbs would be shooting at you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, you were a work platoon of the Semizovac Battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many men did that battalion have?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Rajko Jankovic held two or three lines, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the total number of men in the Semizovac Battalion, how many men in all?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did it have 300 men?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it had more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Let's say between 300 and 400 soldiers, not to over-exaggerate; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, the Semizovac Battalion had a work platoon in which you were, yourself?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The work platoon had 25 members; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that the only work platoon that the Semizovac Battalion had?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only work platoon numbering 25 men, and all trace of them is lost. Only seven or eight of us remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, people get killed in wars, Mr. Sejdic. You must know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, let me stop you. I see the clock ticking. We have to adjourn because I'm sitting in another trial very soon. According to the computations, you have some 20 minutes left. I'll tell you exactly how much time you have left tomorrow. Maybe Mr. Dutertre will have some redirect. So, Witness, as things stand now, you can be sure that your testimony will end tomorrow morning. I thought that we might be done today. Because of a number of problems, we were not able to finish today. Let me tell Mr. Seselj that he has exactly 25 minutes left. We will resume tomorrow at 8.30 a.m. Mr. Seselj will have 25 minutes. Let's hope that there will be no objections and so forth and so on. Then I will give the floor to Mr. Dutertre for the redirect, and we will finish with this witness and then we will have Witness 1012, unless I am mistaken. So, Witness, you are going to come back tomorrow morning, one more day in the courtroom, but rest assured tomorrow your testimony would last at most one hour. So by 9.30, you will be free to go, and you can catch a plane. Thank you, and let's adjourn, and we will resume at 8.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 18th day of June, 2008, at 8.30 a.m. 23 24
